應天府鄉試錄序

天眷皇明，全付以唐虞三代聲教所漸被之舊疆，俾聖子神孫萬世□□之。選賢舉能，以共治天職，祖宗具有成法。

皇上憲天法祖，嗣登寶位以來，天下凡五舉矣。迺成化十六年庚子，又當賓興之歲，應天府府尹臣崇志循例
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination

Heaven favors the august Ming, entrusting it with the entirety of the ancient territories reached by the civilizing influence of Tang Yao, Yu Shun, and the Three Dynasties, so that its sagely sons and divine grandsons might, for ten thousand generations, … them [two illegible characters; sense uncertain]. For selecting the worthy and advancing the capable to share in discharging Heaven’s charge of governance, the imperial ancestors all established precedents.

Since His Majesty, taking Heaven as his model and following his ancestors, succeeded to the treasured throne, examinations have been held throughout the realm five times. Now, in the gengzi year, the sixteenth year of Chenghua [1480], another year has come for honoring and recommending worthy candidates. Your servant Chongzhi, Prefect of Yingtian Prefecture, following established practice …

translation_en:
…sent an urgent memorial requesting Examiners. His Majesty appointed your servants Jing, Librarian, and Dongyang, Expositor-in-waiting. We took our leave in person before the imperial throne and reverently received the favor of an imperially bestowed meal. Together we boarded a postal-service boat and traveled swiftly day and night. Upon our arrival, the Associate Examiners—your servants Tong, Lan, and Huang Lan, Instructors; Lin and Jun, Instructors; and Xuan, Mian, and Jie, Assistant Instructors—the Examination Monitors, your servants Shunbin and Xun, Investigating Censors, and all the functionaries serving inside and outside the examination compound had been engaged or selected to fill their posts. Your servant Chongzhi served as Proctor.
On the jiayin day of the eighth month, the examination compound was sealed. Together with our colleagues, we pledged to devote all our energies to obtaining worthy men for the state. title: 成化十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
未叅以論表諸體壬戌咨以
五策時南畿就試之士總二
千七百有奇前此之所未有
議論彬彬多可觀者猗與盛
哉遵
定制選百三十五人第書其氏
名及三塲文字之尤粹者為
錄錄首當有序臣璟謹拜稽
言曰唐虞三代所以為盛者
三綱五常之道明而已矣漢
唐宋之善政亦多然於三綱
五常之道未盡明是以治不
古若洪惟我
太祖高皇帝繼天立極肇分華夷

===

三綱五常之道明而已矣漢

五常之道未盡明是以治不

punctuated: 未，叅以論、表諸體；壬戌，咨以五策。時南畿就試之士總二千七百有奇，前此之所未有。議論彬彬，多可觀者，猗與盛哉！遵定制，選百三十五人，第書其氏名及三塲文字之尤粹者為錄。錄首當有序，臣璟謹拜稽言曰：唐虞三代所以為盛者，三綱五常之道明而已矣。漢唐宋之善政亦多，然於三綱五常之道未盡明，是以治不古若。洪惟我太祖高皇帝，繼天立極，肇分華夷，
translation_en:
…on the jiwei day, they were further tested in such forms as the discourse and memorial; on the renxu day, they were questioned through five policy questions. At this examination, the candidates from the Southern Metropolitan Region numbered more than 2,700, an unprecedented total. Their arguments displayed refinement and substance, and many were worthy of attention. Ah, what a flourishing age! In accordance with the established regulations, 135 men were selected. Their names were recorded in order, together with the finest writings from the three examination sessions, to form this record.

The record should begin with a preface. Your servant Jing respectfully bows and kowtows, saying: The flourishing of the ages of Tang Yao and Yu Shun and of the Three Dynasties came simply from the clarity of the Way of the Three Bonds and Five Constants. The Han, Tang, and Song also had many instances of good government, but they did not fully illuminate the Way of the Three Bonds and Five Constants. Thus their governance did not equal that of antiquity. Reverently considering our Emperor Taizu Gao, he succeeded Heaven and established the supreme standard, initiating the distinction between the Chinese and the non-Chinese peoples…

title: 成化十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
滌宇宙之腥羶扶綱常於既
墜申明堯舜禹湯文武治天
下之大法三綱五常之道昭
如也
列聖相承所以維持天下者咸用
斯道
皇上近命儒臣續資治通鑑綱目
===
又所以續明斯道也蓋綱常
之道既明則萬事可隨而理
百官萬民由此而正忠直回
邪由此而辨誠為政之首務
有志者之所當深察焉者也
今日之土地即唐虞三代之土
地

墜中明堯舜禹湯文武治天
下之大法三綱五常之道昭
如也

斯道
皇上近命儒臣續資治通鑑綱目
===
又所以續明斯道也蓋綱常
之道既明則萬事可隨而理
百官萬民由此而正忠壹回
邪由此而辨誠為致之首務
有志者之所當深察焉者也
今日之土地即唐虞三代之土
地
punctuated:
滌宇宙之腥羶，扶綱常於既墜，申明堯舜禹湯文武治天下之大法，三綱五常之道昭如也。列聖相承，所以維持天下者咸用斯道。皇上近命儒臣續《資治通鑑綱目》，又所以續明斯道也。蓋綱常之道既明，則萬事可隨而理，百官萬民由此而正，忠直回邪由此而辨，誠為政之首務，有志者之所當深察焉者也。
今日之土地，即唐虞三代之土地。
translation_en:
…cleansed the universe of its rank and rancid taint, upheld the Three Bonds and Five Constants after their collapse, and elucidated the great principles by which Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu governed the realm. Thus the Way of the Three Bonds and Five Constants shone clearly. The successive sage emperors have all employed this Way to sustain the realm. His Majesty recently commanded Confucian officials to continue the Outline and Details of the Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government (Zizhi tongjian gangmu), thereby further illuminating this Way. For once the Way of the Three Bonds and Five Constants is made clear, all affairs can accordingly be brought into order. Through it, the officials and the people are set right; through it, the loyal and upright are distinguished from the devious and wicked. This is truly the foremost task of government, which those with high aspirations ought to examine deeply.
The land of today is the very land of the ages of Yao and Shun and of the Three Dynasties.

title: 成化十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
今日之人心即唐虞三代之人
心上有堯舜禹湯文武之
聖君下必有唐虞三代之賢臣諸
士子皆
國家根本之地之所産毓山川
之靈秀荷仁義之漸摩際
亨嘉之會而出平生所學有大
===
於扶植綱常者乎家居則以
此自考從政則以此為先為
臣必忠為子必孝卓卓乎必
為一時偉人以壮我
國家之元氣使天下後世稱我
朝人才真可擬唐虞三代矣然
後不辱賢科苟曲學阿世若

punctuated: 今日之人心，即唐虞三代之人心。上有堯舜禹湯文武之聖君，下必有唐虞三代之賢臣。諸士子皆國家根本之地之所産毓，山川之靈秀，荷仁義之漸摩，際亨嘉之會，而出平生所學，有大於扶植綱常者乎？家居則以此自考，從政則以此為先。為臣必忠，為子必孝，卓卓乎必為一時偉人，以壮我國家之元氣，使天下後世稱我朝人才真可擬唐虞三代矣，然後不辱賢科。苟曲學阿世，若
translation_en: The hearts of people today are the very same as those of people in the ages of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties. With a sage ruler above like Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, King Wen, and King Wu, there must be worthy ministers below like those of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties. You examination candidates were all born and nurtured in the land that forms the foundation of the state, embodying the finest spiritual essence of its mountains and rivers. Having benefited from the gradual cultivation of benevolence and righteousness, and encountering a felicitous time when worthy men come together, you now bring forth what you have learned throughout your lives. Is there any greater undertaking than sustaining the cardinal relationships and constant virtues? When living at home, measure yourselves by these; when serving in government, put these first. As ministers, you must be loyal; as sons, you must be filial. You must distinguish yourselves as outstanding men of your age, strengthening the vital force of our state and causing all under Heaven and generations to come to declare that the talent of our dynasty truly rivals that of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties. Only then will you bring no dishonor upon the examination for selecting the worthy. If, however, you distort your learning to curry favor with the age, like…

title: 成化十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
漢平津之為者
國家何賴焉孔子曰臣事君以
忠又曰事君敬其事而後其
食此萬世為人臣者之律令
也敢申告於被薦之初
奉訓大夫司經局洗馬羅璟
謹序
alt_text:
漢平津之爲者
國家何賴焉孔子曰臣事君以
忠又曰事君敬其事而後其
食此萬世爲人臣者之律令
也敢申告於被薦之初
奉訓大夫司經局洗馬羅璟
謹序
punctuated:
漢平津之為者，國家何賴焉？孔子曰：「臣事君以忠。」又曰：「事君，敬其事而後其食。」此萬世為人臣者之律令也，敢申告於被薦之初。
奉訓大夫、司經局洗馬羅璟謹序。
translation_en:
…as did the Marquis of Pingjin of the Han, how could the state rely on them? Confucius said, “A minister serves his ruler with loyalty.” He also said, “In serving the ruler, attend reverently to your duties and put your emoluments afterward.” These are binding rules for ministers for all generations. I venture to reiterate them to you upon your initial recommendation.
This preface is respectfully composed by Luo Jing, Grand Master for Exemplary Instruction and Librarian in the Classics Library.

Proctor:
Lu Chongzhi, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel and Prefect of Yingtian Prefecture. His courtesy name was Maogong; he was from Tiantai County, Zhejiang, and was a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the jiaxu year.

title: 成化十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
孝者所以事君也弟者所以事長也慈者
所以使衆也
仁以為己任不亦重乎
由堯舜至於湯五百有餘歳若禹臯陶則
見而知之若湯則聞而知之由湯至
於文王五百有餘歳若伊尹萊朱則
見而知之若文王則聞而知之由文
===
王至於孔子五百有餘歳若太公望
散宜生則見而知之若孔子則聞而
知之
易
飛龍在天乃位乎天德
或益之十朋之龜弗克違永貞吉
動靜有常剛柔斷矣
履和而至謙尊而光復小而辨於物恒雜
而不厭損先難而後易益長裕而不

punctuated:
第壹場

四書

孝者，所以事君也；弟者，所以事長也；慈者，所以使衆也。

仁以為己任，不亦重乎？

由堯舜至於湯，五百有餘歳。若禹、臯陶，則見而知之；若湯，則聞而知之。由湯至於文王，五百有餘歳。若伊尹、萊朱，則見而知之；若文王，則聞而知之。由文王至於孔子，五百有餘歳。若太公望、散宜生，則見而知之；若孔子，則聞而知之。

易

飛龍在天，乃位乎天德。

或益之十朋之龜，弗克違，永貞吉。

動靜有常，剛柔斷矣。

履，和而至；謙，尊而光；復，小而辨於物；恒，雜而不厭；損，先難而後易；益，長裕而不
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

Filial devotion is the means by which one serves one’s ruler; respect for elder brothers is the means by which one serves one’s elders; parental kindness is the means by which one directs the multitude.

To take humaneness as one’s own responsibility—is this not a heavy burden?

From Yao and Shun to Tang, there were more than five hundred years. Such men as Yu and Gao Yao knew their Way through seeing them; Tang knew it through hearing of them. From Tang to King Wen, there were more than five hundred years. Such men as Yi Yin and Lai Zhu knew his Way through seeing him; King Wen knew it through hearing of him. From King Wen to Confucius, there were more than five hundred years. Such men as Taigong Wang and San Yisheng knew his Way through seeing him; Confucius knew it through hearing of him.

Book of Changes

“A flying dragon in heaven”: he thus occupies his position through heavenly virtue.

Someone bestows upon him a tortoise worth ten pairs of cowrie strings; he cannot refuse it. Lasting steadfastness brings good fortune.

Movement and stillness have their constant patterns; the firm and the yielding are thereby distinguished.

Treading (Lü) is harmonious and reaches its goal; Modesty (Qian) is honored and radiant; Return (Fu) is small yet distinguishes among things; Constancy (Heng) encounters complexity yet does not weary; Decrease (Sun) brings difficulty first and ease afterward; Increase (Yi) brings lasting abundance and does not …

大糦是承邦畿千里維民所止肇域

談。困，窮而通；井，居其所而遷；巽，稱而隱。

書
肇十有二州，封十有二山，濬川。
乃審厥象，俾以形旁求于天下。說築傅巖之野，惟肖。
王命予來，承保乃文祖受命民，越乃光烈考武王。
穆穆在上，明明在下。

詩
樂只君子，福履成之。
如山如阜，如岡如陵，如川之方至，以莫不增。
君子萬年，景命有僕。
古帝命武湯，正域彼四方。方命厥后，奄有九有。商之先后，受命不殆，在武丁孫子。武丁孫子，武王靡不勝。龍旂十乘，大糦是承。邦畿千里，維民所止。肇域
translation_en:
…speaking [?]. Confinement means being straitened yet finding a way through; the Well remains in its place yet moves; the Gentle makes things manifest yet remains hidden.

Book of Documents
He first established twelve provinces, marked out twelve mountains, and dredged the rivers.
He then carefully examined the likeness and ordered a search throughout the realm using this portrait. Yue, who was building walls in the countryside of Fuyan, matched it.
The king commanded me to come and undertake the protection of the people over whom your cultured ancestor received the Mandate, and of your illustrious, meritorious father, King Wu.
Reverent and dignified were those above; discerning and enlightened were those below.

Book of Odes
Joyful is the noble lord; blessings bring him fulfillment.
Like mountains and hills, like ridges and high mounds, like a river whose waters are rising, may there be nothing that does not increase.
May the noble lord live ten thousand years; may the great Mandate remain attached to him.

Question: Those who establish a foundation that cannot be uprooted for ten thousand generations must have laws that can be upheld for ten thousand generations. The laws of the Three Dynasties may be called comprehensive. Yet when the Qin of the Ying clan arose, it destroyed them utterly. Han Gaozu’s plans were broad and far-reaching, yet he did not apply himself to the Odes and Documents, and his institutions were hastily devised. Can you set forth the imperfections in his laws? Since the invention of writing, every instance of good government by emperors and kings praised in historical accounts was weighed against the needs of the times and considered in his sagely mind. Matters internal and external, fundamental and subsidiary, great and small, fine and coarse were all set down in authoritative statutes to be handed down for ten thousand generations. He may indeed be said to have brought the achievements of emperors and kings to their fullest realization. Moreover, in moments of leisure amid his myriad affairs, he compiled the three collections of the Great Pronouncements (Da Gao) and the fourteen chapters of Comprehensive Admonitions to Aid the World (Zishi Tongxun), to instruct and admonish his subjects. If his sagely sons and divine grandsons through ten thousand generations preserve the established laws of the Sagely Ancestor, the Nine Provinces and Four Seas will remain free from anxiety for ten thousand generations. Those who aspire to serve the needs of the world must understand this. You candidates have grown up in the metropolitan region. 心存心有先後乎同一聖人也或小心

大人之心何以同於赤子告子之不動

問：人之所以參天地而為三才者，惟一心耳。古聖賢之論心多矣，試舉其一二，相與講之。曰：「人心惟危，道心惟微。」人心、道心果有二乎？曰：「盡心知性，存心養性。」盡心、存心有先後乎？同一聖人也，或小心翼翼，或從心所欲，果同乎？同一君子也，或謂其夕惕若，或謂其坦蕩蕩，果異乎？惻隱、羞惡、辭讓、是非之心，人所必有也，何知之而多不能充？忿懥、恐懼、好樂、憂患，人所不能無也，何有之即不得其正？大人之心何以同於赤子？告子之不動心何以先於孟氏？既曰天地以生物為心，又曰天地無心而成化，何相戾歟？既曰心有所主則虛，又曰心有所主則實，何不一歟？養心莫善於寡欲，與養心莫善於誠者，何殊？以心使心，與以心觀心
translation_en:
…how diligently you have studied matters of the present dynasty in your daily pursuits.

Question: It is solely through the mind that human beings stand alongside Heaven and Earth to constitute the Three Powers. The ancient sages and worthies said much about the mind. Let us select one or two of their statements and discuss them together. It is said: “The human mind is precarious; the mind of the Way is subtle.” Are the human mind and the mind of the Way really two distinct minds? It is said: “Fully realize your mind and know your nature; preserve your mind and nurture your nature.” Is there an order of precedence between fully realizing the mind and preserving it? Both describe a sage: one is cautious and reverent, while another follows his heart’s desires. Are they truly alike? Both describe a gentleman: one is said to remain watchful even in the evening, while another is said to be composed and at ease. Are they truly different?

Everyone necessarily possesses the feelings of compassion, shame and aversion to wrongdoing, deference and yielding, and the sense of right and wrong. Why do so many recognize these yet fail to develop them fully? Anger, fear, fondness, and anxiety are things no one can be entirely without. Why, then, does their presence prevent the mind from attaining its proper state? Why is the mind of a great man the same as that of an infant? Why did Gaozi attain an unperturbed mind before Mengzi? It is said both that Heaven and Earth take the generation of living things as their mind and that Heaven and Earth accomplish transformation without a mind. Why do these statements contradict each other? It is said both that the mind is empty when it has a governing principle and that the mind is substantial when it has a governing principle. Why are these statements inconsistent? What is the difference between saying that nothing is better for nurturing the mind than reducing desires and saying that nothing is better for nurturing the mind than sincerity? Using the mind to direct the mind, and using the mind to observe the mind…

…what distinguishes them? The heart governed by heavenly principle should be pure; why, then, could someone endowed with the qualities of the Second Sage still not avoid departing from benevolence after three months? The heart’s selfish desires should be overcome; why, then, could someone of a great worthy’s learning still not rid himself of the desire to hunt after as long as twelve years? Whom, indeed, should those who aspire to the learning of the heart today take as their teacher, and how should they exert themselves? All these matters inevitably raise doubts. Surely scholars who understand words can distinguish among them. We wish to hear a detailed explanation.
Question: In handling the affairs of the world, there must always be an appropriate course. Yet observing the conduct of the ancients has given rise to doubts. To ask the Metropolitan Superintendent about money and grain, and the Chamberlain for Law Enforcement about deciding legal cases, was considered a sound account of the chief councilor’s role. Yet entrusting personnel and ritual affairs to Yanshang, and penal law to Yu, was considered unacceptable. Maintaining tranquility, with no business troubling the government office [preceding wording unclear: 分載其清靜], was considered skillful service as chief councilor. Yet one who personally checked registers and documents, sweating all day, understood this but could not change his ways. There was one who requested the abolition of duplicate sealed submissions; yet one who burned memorials in an earthenware jar concealed them so that they were not heard of. There was one who refused to use confidential submissions; yet one who selected officials through written submissions first settled on his choices and only afterward reported them to the throne. One said that he wished to follow Feng and Gan; another said that he wished to be a Gao or a Kui. One recommended worthy men for the state rather than for private interests; another openly promoted scholars, yet was deficient in this alone. Why were their actions so different? text:
政雖大臣莫知者矣而兄弟燕語不及
政事者有之有佐君獨斷雖舉朝莫奪
者矣而力主新法不恤人言者有之有
十說玄宗而後拜相有三奏高宗而後
議和有不欲補外入守少府者有被罷
願留自全中書者布被之詰則曰黯忠
政府之短則曰準直登聞之命則曰願
入恐其不靜也諫官之舉則曰介入恐
其責難也是何其事之同邪夫人皆賢
===
也而所施異其事相似也而所出異
其人不可以不辨也是將以一言蓋一
人一事蓋一時者非邪抑猶有同而異
異而同者存乎其間邪即已行之事以
求當然之義則其言也非出位之言也
試為我言之
問以學校育材以科目取士此
國朝斟酌三代漢唐宋之良法而行之者也
今日輔理承化庶司百府之賢胥此焉出可

translation_en:
…major affairs of government, without even the high ministers knowing of them; yet there were also those whose private conversations with their brothers never touched upon government affairs. There were those who assisted their sovereign in making independent decisions that the entire court could not overturn; yet there were also those who vigorously supported the New Policies without regard for what others said. One persuaded Xuanzong ten times before being appointed chief minister; another submitted three memorials to Gaozong before peace negotiations were undertaken. One, unwilling to receive a provincial appointment, entered service as Chamberlain for the Palace Revenues; another, after being dismissed, wished to remain and secure his position in the Secretariat [?]. When challenged about the cloth coverlet, the reply was, “An was loyal”; when shortcomings in the chief councillors’ administration were raised, the reply was, “Zhun was upright.” Regarding an appointment to the office for receiving petitions, it was said, “If Yuan [?] enters, I fear he will not keep quiet”; regarding a nomination as a remonstrance official, it was said, “If Jie enters, I fear he will demand what is difficult.” How alike these affairs seem! These men were all worthy, yet differed in what they put into practice; their actions resembled one another, yet differed in their motives. We must distinguish among the men. Is it therefore wrong to judge a person by a single remark, or an entire period by a single incident? Or do similarities that conceal differences, and differences that conceal similarities, still lie among these cases? If you examine actions already taken to seek the principles of what ought to be done, your remarks will not constitute speaking beyond your station. Explain this for me.

text:
謂盛矣然古今事宜亦有所當知者夫
建學明倫教養之法以行成周之為教
有所謂小成大成而屏其不率教者其
法何如漢唐之教在於儒師有明辨經
義諸儒莫及者有解經不窮召為侍中

蘇湖分置經義治事諸齋其說可得聞

今日學校既專之以師儒又董之以憲臣設
置科條皆先德行後文藝之事然勸懲
於筆札記誦之間果足以盡教之之道
乎舎此則又何以驗其進修賓興論秀
豪傑所由以出成周以鄉三物教萬民
而興其賢者能者其制何若漢唐諸賢

translation_en:
…may be called flourishing indeed. Yet there are matters concerning what is appropriate to past and present that one ought also to understand. By establishing schools and clarifying human relationships, methods of instruction and nurture are put into practice. In the educational system of the Zhou, there were what were called “minor attainment” and “major attainment,” and those who would not follow the instruction were excluded. What were these methods? Under the Han and Tang, education rested with Confucian teachers. There were those whose clear discrimination of the meanings of the Classics was unmatched by other scholars; those whose inexhaustible exposition of the Classics earned them summonses to serve as Palace Attendants; those whose conduct set a standard and whose words and actions were emulated; and those who encouraged goodness and restrained faults, being sincere, kindly, and amiable. Which of these men was superior? In the teaching of the Song Confucians, separate study halls for the meaning of the Classics and practical administration were established in Suzhou and Huzhou. May we hear an account of this?
Today, schools are entrusted specifically to Confucian teachers and are also overseen by censorial officials. Their established regulations all place moral conduct before literary accomplishment. Yet can encouragement and correction through writing, memorization, and recitation truly fulfill the entire purpose of teaching? Apart from these, how else can students’ progress in learning and self-cultivation be assessed? Honoring worthy candidates as guests and evaluating outstanding talent are the means by which exceptional men emerge. The Zhou taught all the people through the three categories of instruction in the townships and promoted the worthy and capable among them. What was this system like? Among the worthies of the Han and Tang who emerged through selection categories, there were those whose exposition of the Book of Odes brought delighted smiles and who boldly submitted memorials discussing affairs; those who understood the Classics, were steady and circumspect, and possessed the ability to serve as chief ministers; those who rejected Buddhism and Daoism and whose writings were revered like Mount Tai and the Northern Dipper; and those who offered arguments and remonstrances grounded in benevolence and righteousness, living up to what they had learned. Among them …

title: 成化十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
人爲孰勝宋儒之議貢舉欲分經史爲
諸科其議可得詳乎
今日科目雖嚴于防範去取之法實隆夫勸
駕續食之禮文移保覈亦先里選後考
校之意然選擇於風簷寸晷之作果足
以盡取人之方乎舍此則又何以爲之
衡度爾諸士皆育秀學校茲將籍科目
以出矣必有至論以助有司
問古之論爲國者曰食與兵此二者相須
===
===
而不可闕者也夫兵民之判久矣今不
暇遠引姑以時之切務言之南畿多良
田而賦亦仍舊宜其足供也而往往有
闕賦之夫北畿多閒田而賦又甚薄宜
其足耕也而在在有無田之室賑貸美
意也而貧民或不蒙其惠勸借權法也
而富室或并受其菑儲蓄長計也而有
司或虛有其籍此又天下之通弊也茲
欲使民之家必給人必足雖有水旱不

translation_en:
…which of these men was superior? When Song Confucian scholars discussed the system of recommending and examining candidates, they proposed dividing the Classics and histories into separate examination subjects. Can their proposals be explained in detail? Although today’s examination system has strict rules for preventing abuses and accepting or rejecting candidates, it also accords great importance to the rites of encouraging candidates to proceed to the examination and providing them with food along the way. The circulation of official documents and the verification of guarantees likewise embody the intention of selecting men locally before examining them. Yet can selection based on compositions written under windswept eaves within a brief allotted time truly fulfill all the requirements for recruiting worthy men? If this method is abandoned, what else can serve as a standard for judging them? You scholars have all nurtured your talents in the schools and are now about to enter public service through the examinations. Surely you have well-considered arguments to assist the responsible officials.

Question: Those in antiquity who discussed governing a state spoke of food and troops. These two depend upon each other, and neither can be dispensed with. Soldiers and civilians have long been separate. There is no time now to cite distant precedents; let us speak instead of the pressing concerns of the present. The Southern Metropolitan Region has much good farmland, and its tax assessments remain as before: one would expect it to supply enough revenue, yet there are frequently men who fall short in their tax payments. The Northern Metropolitan Region has much unused land, and its tax assessments are very light: one would expect there to be enough land to cultivate, yet everywhere there are households without fields. Relief grants and loans are benevolent in intention, yet poor people sometimes receive none of their benefits. Encouraging loans from the wealthy is an expedient measure, yet wealthy households sometimes suffer calamity as well. Building reserves is a long-term strategy, yet the responsible officials sometimes have only empty entries in their registers. These, too, are abuses common throughout the realm. We now wish to ensure that every household has enough and every person is adequately provided for, so that even floods and droughts would not…

title: 成化十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
足爲害何道而宜嶺海之間蠻夷之率
服久矣然必有區畫之方關塞之外戎
虜之挫衂屢矣然必有備禦之策肄練
有法而作止或有未齊勾稽有籍而什
伍或有未實稟給有制而衣食或有未
充此亦天下之恒事也茲欲使兵之戰
必勝守必固雖有外警不足以為患何
施而效夫水旱者堯湯之所不能免也
夷狄者三代之所不能無也然則先事
===
而為之慮及時而為之圖以求所謂久
安長治者苟有經濟之志宜於此焉熟
矣其悉陳之毋隱

而爲之處及時而爲之圖以求所謂久
安長治者茍有經濟之志宜於此焉熟
矣其悉陳之毋隱
punctuated: 足爲害，何道而宜？嶺海之間，蠻夷之率服久矣，然必有區畫之方；關塞之外，戎虜之挫衂屢矣，然必有備禦之策。肄練有法，而作止或有未齊；勾稽有籍，而什伍或有未實；稟給有制，而衣食或有未充。此亦天下之恒事也。茲欲使兵之戰必勝、守必固，雖有外警，不足以為患，何施而效？夫水旱者，堯湯之所不能免也；夷狄者，三代之所不能無也。然則先事而為之慮，及時而為之圖，以求所謂久安長治者，苟有經濟之志，宜於此焉熟矣。其悉陳之，毋隱。
translation_en:
…insufficient to cause harm: what course would be appropriate? In the region between the mountain ranges and the sea, the Man and Yi peoples have long submitted to our rule; nevertheless, there must be a method for organizing and administering the region. Beyond the frontier passes, the Rong invaders have repeatedly suffered defeat; nevertheless, there must be a strategy for defensive preparations. There are methods for military training, yet movements and halts may still lack coordination; there are registers for checking personnel, yet the units of five and ten may still lack their actual complement; there are regulations for issuing provisions, yet clothing and food may still be insufficient. These, too, are persistent conditions throughout the realm. Now, if we wish to ensure that our troops invariably win when they fight and hold firm when they defend, so that even alarms from abroad are insufficient to cause trouble, what measures would prove effective?

Floods and droughts were calamities that even Yao and Tang could not avoid; the Yi and Di peoples were a presence that even the Three Dynasties could not eliminate. Thus, one must consider matters before they arise and devise plans in good time, seeking what is called enduring peace and lasting good government. Anyone with the ambition to order the realm and aid its people should have reflected thoroughly on these matters. Set forth your views in full, withholding nothing.

title: 成化十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
孝者所以事君也弟者所以事長也慈者
所以使衆也
貢欽
同考試官訓導范批大學一題不過言
家國一道耳作者體認不真或以推言或以
效言殊戾厥旨是作一破既佳且講貫明白
允宜錄出
===
同考試官學正黃批此篇說出三所以
字親切有味蓋嘗究心於經傳視場中泛泛者
不侔矣
考試官侍講李批文能說理集註意正如
此
考試官洗馬羅批得旨
舉身教之三端明家國之一道蓋孝弟慈三者
人道之大端也君子以之修身而教於家則國
之所以事君事長使衆之道又豈外於是哉昔

…Zengzi, in his commentary on the Great Learning, explained why governing the state must begin with ordering one’s family. He said that the gentleman completes his teaching in the state without going beyond his family, and proceeded to discuss how he teaches through his own conduct. His meaning was this: toward the parents in one’s family, one should show filial devotion. When the gentleman serves his parents with reverent apprehension and utmost effort, he thinks only of fulfilling his filial duty and thereby teaching within his family. Yet the way to serve one’s ruler in the state, devoting oneself without slackening morning or night, is present in this very conduct. Who could say that the way of serving a ruler lies outside filial devotion? Toward elder brothers in one’s family, one should show fraternal deference. When the gentleman serves his elder brothers with unfailing reverence and respect, he thinks only of fulfilling his fraternal duty and thereby teaching within his family. Yet the way to serve one’s superiors in the state with humility, modesty, deference, and obedience is present in this very conduct. Who could say that the way of serving superiors lies outside fraternal deference? As for the young in one’s family, one should show them kindness. When the gentleman cares for the young by caressing and nurturing them, leading them by the hand and holding them protectively in his arms, he likewise thinks only of fully expressing his kindness and thereby teaching within his family. Yet the way to direct the multitude in the state, bringing relief to widowers and widows and cherishing and protecting the common people, is likewise present in this very conduct. Who, then, could say that the way of directing the multitude lies outside kindness?
Ah! Here Zengzi does not say that filial devotion is the means of serving one’s parents, but that it is the means of serving one’s ruler; he does not say that fraternal deference is the means of serving one’s elder brothers, but that it is the means of serving one’s superiors; he does not say that kindness is the means of caring for the young, but that it is the means of directing the multitude. Is this not precisely to show that family and state follow one and the same principle, and that ordering the family and governing the state are not two separate ways—so that, through the ordering of the family above, teaching is accomplished below [?]? One must examine and experience it within one’s thoughts and faithfully enact it in everyday conduct. In movement and stillness, speech and silence, one must abide in humaneness. If my humaneness falls short of complete realization by so much as a hair’s breadth, my heart feels dissatisfied, as though I had failed an obligation; I must seek its complete realization before I rest. In haste and distress, one must abide in humaneness. If my humaneness falls short of attainment by even the slightest degree, my heart grows apprehensive, as though I had lost something; I must seek its full attainment before I stop. Such is the scholar’s taking humaneness as his own charge. But how can we see that this charge is heavy?

As a virtue, humaneness is so great that nothing is greater. To undertake its greatness in my own person without declining it—can this fail to be called a heavy charge? The work of practicing humaneness is so difficult that nothing is more difficult. To hold myself personally responsible for this difficulty and insist on fulfilling the task—can this, too, fail to be called a heavy charge? Even minor affairs require someone to undertake them before they can be accomplished. Now, when I take humaneness as my charge, all the goodness under Heaven converges in me. What charge could be as heavy? Even lesser virtues require someone to assume responsibility for them before they can be put into practice. Now, when I take humaneness as my responsibility, all the principles under Heaven are borne by me. What charge could be as heavy? Such is the weight of the scholar’s charge. text:
之在當時聞之者之在後世則斯道也孰從而
傳之哉孟子於此而歷叙之意有在矣蓋嘗論
之道之在天下必待聖人而後傳然其生也不
數故率以五百年而一見堯舜者道之所由以
傳者也自堯舜以至於湯以其年計之則五百
有餘也當是時見而知其道者禹得之於執中
之命皐陶得之為典禮之謨若湯之生也則聞
其道而知之焉觀於上帝降衷之言則斯道之
統在於湯矣自湯至於文王以其年計之亦五

translation_en: …being present in their own time, and those who knew by hearing being present in later generations, through whom, then, could this Way be transmitted? Mengzi had a purpose in recounting this succession here. Let us consider it: the Way in the world must await sages before it can be transmitted. Yet sages are born infrequently; thus, as a rule, one appears every five hundred years. Yao and Shun were those through whom the Way was transmitted. Counting the years from Yao and Shun down to Tang gives more than five hundred. Among those who knew their Way by seeing them at that time, Yu grasped it in the injunction to hold fast to the mean, and Gao Yao grasped it and expressed it in counsels concerning established institutions and rites. When Tang was born, he knew their Way by hearing of it. Looking at his words about the Lord on High bestowing an upright nature, we see that the succession of this Way rested with Tang. From Tang to King Wen, the count likewise exceeds five hundred years. Among those who knew the Way by seeing Tang at that time, Yi Yin grasped it and served as an assistant of single-minded virtue; Lai Zhu grasped it and expressed it in an admonition on establishing the mean. When King Wen was born, he knew the Way by hearing of it. Looking at the poem describing his continuing brightness and abiding reverence, we see that the succession of this Way rested with King Wen. From King Wen to Kongzi there were likewise more than five hundred years, just as from Yao and Shun to Tang, and from Tang to King Wen. Among those who knew the Way by seeing King Wen at that time, there was Taigong Wang, who grasped it and expressed it in the admonitions of the Cinnabar Writing; and there was San Yisheng, who grasped it and provided guidance through the constant teachings. When Kongzi was born, he knew the Way by hearing of it. The worthy retained its greater elements, and the less worthy retained its lesser elements; he learned from them all. This was precisely King Wen’s Way. The succession of this Way…

…was not the succession of this Way, in turn, vested in Confucius? Ah! Though their ages came earlier or later, the Way knows no distinction between earlier and later; though its transmission spans distances near and far, the Way knows no difference between near and far. When, then, has this Way ever been absent from the world for even a single day? Moreover, examining this chapter of Mencius, we see that he recounts in sequence the succession of the sages and expresses concern that the transmission of this Way might be lost. In doing so, he reveals that he himself bears a responsibility he cannot decline. Thus, on another occasion he said: “Every five hundred years a true king must arise, and in the interval there must be someone renowned in his age. In the present age, who but myself could it be?” Several hundred years later, Master Han said: “Confucius transmitted it to Meng Ke.” Is this not indeed true?

text:
文言申乾九五之象明聖人以至德而居尊位
也盖有天德而後可以當天位之尊乾之九五
既有其象矣文言安得不申言以發其蘊哉昔
孔子作乾之文言舉周公繫九五之辭謂夫龍
者陽物之靈聖人至德之象也龍而飛焉則其
變化莫測有非初潛二見之可倫矣天者至高
之處人君尊位之象也飛龍而在天焉則其雲
行雨施有非在淵在田之可擬矣孔子既舉周
公之辭又從而賛之曰是象也乃聖人之有是
===
德而宜居是位者也盖其剛而不屈健而不息
德極乎剛健之純無過不及不偏不倚德極乎
中正之粹以是德而尊居九重以君臨乎天下
深仁厚澤徧覆於斯民則是位也非泰也宜也
以是德而升躋大寶以統御乎萬方盛德至善
丕冒於斯世則是位也非過也宜也謂之乃位
乎天德亶其然乎抑論之乾之六爻皆天德也
惟五為天位則天德之得位者也孔子既象之
曰大人造也而於文言又曰聖人作而萬物覩

punctuated: 文言申乾九五之象，明聖人以至德而居尊位也。盖有天德而後可以當天位之尊，乾之九五既有其象矣，文言安得不申言以發其蘊哉？昔孔子作乾之文言，舉周公繫九五之辭，謂夫龍者，陽物之靈，聖人至德之象也。龍而飛焉，則其變化莫測，有非初潛二見之可倫矣。天者，至高之處，人君尊位之象也。飛龍而在天焉，則其雲行雨施，有非在淵在田之可擬矣。孔子既舉周公之辭，又從而賛之曰：「是象也，乃聖人之有是德而宜居是位者也。」盖其剛而不屈，健而不息，德極乎剛健之純；無過不及，不偏不倚，德極乎中正之粹。以是德而尊居九重，以君臨乎天下，深仁厚澤徧覆於斯民，則是位也，非泰也，宜也。以是德而升躋大寶，以統御乎萬方，盛德至善丕冒於斯世，則是位也，非過也，宜也。謂之「乃位乎天德」，亶其然乎！抑論之，乾之六爻皆天德也，惟五為天位，則天德之得位者也。孔子既象之曰：「大人造也。」而於文言又曰：「聖人作而萬物覩」
translation_en:
The Commentary on the Words (Wenyan) elaborates the image of the nine in the fifth place of Qian, explaining how the sage occupies an exalted position by virtue of his utmost virtue. Only after possessing heavenly virtue can one be worthy of the exalted heavenly position. Since the nine in the fifth place of Qian already presents this image, how could the Commentary on the Words fail to elaborate it and reveal its underlying meaning?

When Confucius composed the Commentary on the Words for Qian, he cited the words that the Duke of Zhou attached to the nine in the fifth place. The dragon, he held, is the most numinous of yang creatures and an image of the sage’s utmost virtue. When the dragon flies, its transformations are unfathomable, beyond comparison with its concealment in the first line or its appearance in the second. Heaven is the highest place and an image of the ruler’s exalted position. When the flying dragon is in heaven, clouds move and rain falls through its agency, beyond comparison with its being in the depths or in the fields. Having cited the Duke of Zhou’s words, Confucius further praised them, saying: “This image represents the sage who possesses this virtue and is therefore fit to occupy this position.”

Firm without yielding and vigorous without ceasing, his virtue reaches the perfection of pure firmness and vigor. Neither exceeding nor falling short, neither deviating nor inclining to either side, his virtue reaches the perfection of centrality and correctness. With this virtue he occupies the exalted palace of nine enclosures and reigns over all under heaven; his profound benevolence and abundant beneficence extend over all these people. Thus his position is no undue exaltation: it is fitting. With this virtue he ascends the imperial throne and governs the myriad regions; his flourishing virtue and utmost goodness broadly encompass the world. Thus his position is no excess: it is fitting. How truly it is said of him that he “thus occupies the position of heavenly virtue”!

To consider this further, all six lines of Qian embody heavenly virtue, but only the fifth is the heavenly position: it is heavenly virtue attaining its proper position. Confucius already explained its image by saying, “The great man arises.” In the Commentary on the Words he further says, “The sage arises, and all things behold him…”

text:
皆主於動焉惟陰之生於靜也故凡陰之在天
下為收斂為閉藏為凝滯為停畜者萬有不一
也而皆主於靜焉動者常動而不入於靜其所
以動者非強之也一陽之自然也靜者常靜而
不汩於動其所以靜者非柅之也一陰之自然
也是非造化陰陽之有定者乎及夫聖人作易
因夫陽之動也則有奇以象之而奇者皆剛則
剛於是而斷焉因夫陰之靜也則有耦以象之
而耦者皆柔則柔於是而斷焉自一爻之陽推
===

剛矣自一爻之陰推之至於百九十二之陰爻
凡所謂陰者皆謂之柔矣剛者常剛而不雜於

punctuated: 皆主於動焉。惟陰之生於靜也，故凡陰之在天下，為收斂，為閉藏，為凝滯，為停畜者，萬有不一也，而皆主於靜焉。動者常動而不入於靜，其所以動者，非強之也，一陽之自然也；靜者常靜而不汩於動，其所以靜者，非柅之也，一陰之自然也。是非造化陰陽之有定者乎？及夫聖人作《易》，因夫陽之動也，則有奇以象之，而奇者皆剛，則剛於是而斷焉；因夫陰之靜也，則有耦以象之，而耦者皆柔，則柔於是而斷焉。自一爻之陽推之至於百九十二之陽爻，凡所謂陽者，皆謂之剛矣；自一爻之陰推之至於百九十二之陰爻，凡所謂陰者，皆謂之柔矣。剛者常剛而不雜於柔，一定而不可易也；柔者常柔而不雜於剛，一成而不可變也。是又非卦爻陰陽之有定者乎？大抵《易》與天地準者也，故天尊地卑，則乾坤以定；卑高以陳，則貴賤以位；方以類聚，物以羣分，則吉凶生；在天成象，在地成形，則變化見。皆因陰陽之實體，為卦爻之法象。所謂「易以道陰陽」
translation_en:
…all are governed by movement. Since yin arises from stillness, all its manifestations under Heaven—as contraction, concealment, congealing, or accumulation at rest—have countless variations, yet all are governed by stillness. What moves always moves and does not enter into stillness. Its movement is not forced upon it; it is simply the natural operation of yang. What is still always remains still and is not swept into movement. Its stillness does not result from restraint; it is simply the natural operation of yin. Is this not the fixed character of yin and yang in the work of creation and transformation?

When the sages composed the Book of Changes, they took the movement of yang as their basis and represented it with an undivided line. Undivided lines are all firm, and thus firmness was determined. They took the stillness of yin as their basis and represented it with a divided line. Divided lines are all yielding, and thus yieldingness was determined. Extending from the yang of a single line to all 192 yang lines, everything designated yang is called firm. Extending from the yin of a single line to all 192 yin lines, everything designated yin is called yielding. The firm always remains firm, unmixed with the yielding: once fixed, it cannot be altered. The yielding always remains yielding, unmixed with the firm: once established, it cannot be changed. Is this not, in turn, the fixed character of yin and yang in the hexagrams and their lines?

In general, the Book of Changes accords with Heaven and Earth. Thus, because Heaven is exalted and Earth is lowly, Qian and Kun are established. Because low and high are arrayed, noble and base take their positions. Because activities gather according to kind and things divide into groups, good fortune and misfortune arise. Because images take shape in Heaven and forms take shape on Earth, change and transformation become manifest. All take the actual substance of yin and yang as the basis for the patterned representations of the hexagrams and their lines. As for the saying, “The Book of Changes articulates yin and yang”…

He therefore recalled what he had seen between waking and sleeping, carefully examined the appearance that he alone had witnessed, and had it clearly depicted in a portrait and displayed for all to see. Thus, what had been apprehended dimly would provide a basis for the search, and what was transmitted amid uncertainty would provide a means of verification. When the man could not be found in one region, he sent men to search throughout the four quarters, giving no thought to the distances involved. When inquiries in one state proved fruitless, he sent men to inquire throughout the realm, taking no account of the months and years that might pass.
There was then a man named Fu Yue, living in seclusion in the former territory of Yu and Guo, who had chosen a site for his dwelling in the countryside of Fuyan. As for the place, it was exceedingly remote; as for the man, his station was exceedingly humble. Previously, he had embraced the Way and nurtured virtue, yet the world knew nothing of him. Now, when they took the portrait and checked it against him, the depicted figure was unmistakably this very man. Previously, he had concealed his traces and hidden his brilliance, and no one recognized him. Now, when they approached the man and looked at him, he was the very image of the portrait. Could an event be so extraordinary!
Ah! An omen arose in the subtlest stirrings of thought, and a response came through the wondrous workings of the spirit. 同考試官教諭劉批：《洛誥》一題，本以保民爲誌。作者欠明，甚至是光顯武王功業爲說。此作體認明白，而文又足以發之，是宜錄出。

同考試官教諭方批：題本五文陽守艱見者多，此篇獨能寫出周公許成王留洛之意，明而且暢，非雜筆可到。

考試官侍講李批：講王命、天命處，明暢該括，尤警切。

考試官洗馬羅批：道盡盛時君臣之意。

大臣述賢王留後之意，正以安前王所受之民。蓋民者，君相之所治者也，而況受之於前王、受之於天者，大臣安得不以君命而自任也哉？昔
translation_en:
…through divination was likewise so. Yet this is possible only when rulers are like Gaozong and King Wen, and ministers like Fu Yue and Lü Shang. Alas! The world has never lacked worthy men. If there is sincerity in seeking them, worthy men will be found. Why must one necessarily resort to dreams and divination?

“The king has commanded me to come and continue to protect the people entrusted by Heaven’s mandate to your cultured ancestor and to your illustrious, meritorious deceased father, King Wu.”
Lü Lu

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Instructor: This topic from the “Announcement concerning Luo” fundamentally takes protecting the people as its aim. Writers fail to understand this clearly, even explaining it as glorifying King Wu’s achievements. This composition grasps the meaning clearly, and its prose adequately brings that meaning out. It therefore deserves to be included.

Comment by Associate Examiner Fang, Instructor: The topic’s basis [the following wording is garbled: 五文陽守艱見者多; ?]. This essay alone brings out the Duke of Zhou’s intention in agreeing to King Cheng’s request that he remain at Luo. It is clear and fluent, beyond the reach of miscellaneous writing.

Comment by Examiner Li, Expositor-in-waiting: The passages explaining the king’s command and Heaven’s mandate are clear, fluent, and comprehensive, and especially incisive and pertinent.

Comment by Examiner Luo, Librarian: It fully expresses the intentions of ruler and minister in an age of flourishing government.

The great minister set forth the worthy king’s intention in having him remain behind, precisely in order to bring peace to the people entrusted to the former kings. The people are those whom ruler and chief minister govern. How much more is this so when they have been received from the former kings and from Heaven! How could the great minister fail to take the king’s command as his own responsibility? In former times…

title: 成化十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
夫洛邑既成成王留周公治洛欲其誕保文武
受民於是周公許之若曰夙夜毖祀王欲為之
矣而命我以來此洛邑焉即辟于周王固任之
矣而命我以留此洛邑焉公無困哉之言懇懇
乎其不我釋而明農之志不敢以自遂也公勿
替刑之戒拳拳乎其不我置而留後之責不得
以自辭也王之所以命我者豈無故而然哉誠
以誕受多方文王之受命於天者今洛之民即
文王之民也不有以承保之不幾於負文祖之
===
托乎盖必和輯愛養囿之於綱常倫理之天而
所謂萬民咸和者累世如一日也及夫奄甸萬
姓武王之受命於天者今洛之民即武王之民
也不有以承保之不幾於遏烈考之光乎盖必
綏柔撫定陶之於禮樂教化之域而所謂四海
永清者歷世如一時也然則是民也天以之而
命文武文武以之而命於王王以之而命於予
者如此其重敢不思所以無負於王無忝於祖
考以無愧於天哉抑嘗觀周公之欲歸於周者

所謂萬民咸和者累世如一日也及夫奄甸萬

punctuated:
夫洛邑既成，成王留周公治洛，欲其誕保文武受民。於是周公許之，若曰：「夙夜毖祀，王欲為之矣，而命我以來此洛邑焉；即辟于周，王固任之矣，而命我以留此洛邑焉。公無困哉之言，懇懇乎其不我釋，而明農之志不敢以自遂也；公勿替刑之戒，拳拳乎其不我置，而留後之責不得以自辭也。王之所以命我者，豈無故而然哉？誠以誕受多方，文王之受命於天者，今洛之民即文王之民也。不有以承保之，不幾於負文祖之托乎？盖必和輯愛養，囿之於綱常倫理之天，而所謂萬民咸和者，累世如一日也。及夫奄甸萬姓，武王之受命於天者，今洛之民即武王之民也。不有以承保之，不幾於遏烈考之光乎？盖必綏柔撫定，陶之於禮樂教化之域，而所謂四海永清者，歷世如一時也。然則是民也，天以之而命文武，文武以之而命於王，王以之而命於予者，如此其重，敢不思所以無負於王、無忝於祖考，以無愧於天哉？」
抑嘗觀周公之欲歸於周者，
translation_en:
…when Luoyi had been completed, King Cheng asked the Duke of Zhou to remain and govern Luo, wishing him to give ample protection to the people received by Kings Wen and Wu. The Duke of Zhou consented, as though saying: “To attend reverently to the sacrifices morning and night is what you, O King, intend to do, and you command me to come here to Luoyi. To occupy the throne at Zhou is indeed your responsibility, and you command me to remain here in Luoyi. In saying, ‘Duke, do not weary yourself,’ you earnestly refuse to release me, so I dare not fulfill my own wish to retire to farming. In admonishing me, ‘Duke, do not abandon the established models,’ you devotedly refuse to let me go, so I cannot decline the responsibility of remaining behind. Could your command to me be without reason?
“Truly, King Wen received Heaven’s mandate to receive the many regions on a grand scale; the people of Luo today are King Wen’s people. If I fail to carry on their protection, would I not come close to betraying the trust of your cultivated ancestor? I must bring them into harmony, cherish and nurture them, and encompass them within the heaven of the cardinal bonds, constant virtues, and ethical relationships, so that what is called ‘all the people dwelling in harmony’ may endure through successive generations as though they were a single day. Then King Wu received Heaven’s mandate to govern all the myriad surnames; the people of Luo today are King Wu’s people. If I fail to carry on their protection, would I not come close to dimming the glory of your illustrious father? I must soothe and settle them, forming them within the realm of rites, music, instruction, and moral transformation, so that what is called ‘the Four Seas forever tranquil’ may endure through successive generations as though they were a single moment.
“Thus, these people were entrusted by Heaven to Wen and Wu, by Wen and Wu to you, O King, and by you to me. So weighty is this charge: dare I fail to consider how to avoid disappointing you or dishonoring your ancestors, and thereby stand without shame before Heaven?”
“Yet I have considered the Duke of Zhou’s wish to return to Zhou…

宜周公之許之也厥後誕保文武受命七年而
終身焉式化厥訓效亦盛矣成周八百年之治

translation_en:
…was the sage’s resolve to recognize when to retire; his remaining once more at Luo expressed an old minister’s sense of duty toward the state. King Cheng retained him not merely for his own sake, but for the sake of Kings Wen and Wu and of Heaven’s mandate. It was fitting that the Duke of Zhou should agree. Thereafter he amply safeguarded the mandate received by Wen and Wu, through seven years and to the end of his life [?]. Taking his teachings as a model and being transformed by them yielded splendid results. There was indeed a reason for the Zhou dynasty’s eight hundred years of orderly rule!

Book of Odes
“May the lord live ten thousand years; may the great mandate attach to him.”
Su Xin

Comment by Associate Examiner Fan, Assistant Instructor: Responses to this question from the Greater Odes were either prolix or wooden, with little development of its meaning. This essay unfolds the classic’s meaning, excelling in both expression and reasoning. It merits inclusion.

Comment by Associate Examiner Huang, Instructor: There were no fewer than a thousand examination papers on the Odes. Those addressing this question were mostly hampered by “may the great mandate attach to him,” becoming verbose, vague, and irrelevant. Only this essay succeeds in conveying how the poet recounts the words of blessing to wish that his lord might long enjoy Heaven’s favor, thereby laying the foundation for the prosperity of later generations.

Comment by Examiner Li, Expositor-in-waiting: Composed with ease and without haste: this is indeed how an exposition of the Odes should be written.

Comment by Examiner Luo, Editorial Director: Its meaning is clear and its language lucid. Here is someone who explains the Odes well.

The poet recounts the words of blessing to bless his lord, wishing only that he might long enjoy his allotted span of rule and that Heaven’s mandate might attach to him. For when Heaven’s mandate attaches to him, extending to a duration of ten thousand years …

title: 成化十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
久此錫胤之本也詩人述嘏辭以是而祝君忠
愛之意為何如哉昔有周盛時父兄耆老承行
葦之燕賦此詩以答其君至是蓋曰公尸言將
使爾有子孫者先當使爾被天祿而為天命之
所附屬焉其必俾吾君之永膺乎曆數萬有千
歲綿綿不絕而非月日之可期其必俾吾君之
永受乎天祿於萬斯年勿替引之而非歲時之
可計惟曆數之永膺則假哉天命降于冥冥之
中以附集吾君者亦萬年而無替寧有一時之
===
暫離乎惟天祿之永受則有命自天運于蒼蒼
之表以附屬吾君者亦萬年而無已寧有一時
之暫舍乎夫以天命而附集於萬年之永則所
謂錫之以胤者蓋非一朝一夕之故矣吁周之
父兄亦可謂善於祝頌者歟抑考其詩此章既
曰景命有僕下章申所謂僕者則曰釐爾女士從
以孫子蓋言天命之所附屬不過予爾以賢女
使為之妃又隨之生賢子孫焉耳合行葦而觀
之則周王頌禱於父兄與父兄祝頌於周王者

久此錫胤之本也詩人述嘏辭以是而祝君忠
愛之意爲何如哉昔有周盛時父兄耆老承衎
幕之燕賦此詩以答其君至是蓋因公尸言將

可計惟曆數之永膺則假哉天命降于寘寘之
中以附集吾君者亦萬年而無□□有一時之
===
暫離乎惟天祿之永受則有命□天運于蒼蒼
之表以附屬吾君者亦萬年而□□□有二時
之暫舍乎夫以天命而附□□□之永則所
謂錫之以胤者蓋非一朝一□之□矣吁闕之
文見亦可謂善於祝頌者□□□□□□章既
曰景命有僕下章申所謂僕者□□□□於士
以孫子蓋言天命之所附屬不過于□□以賢女
使爲之妃又隨之生賢子孫爲耳合於當而觀
之則周王頌禱於父兄□□□□□□於周王者
punctuated:
久，此錫胤之本也。詩人述嘏辭，以是而祝君，忠愛之意為何如哉！昔有周盛時，父兄耆老承《行葦》之燕，賦此詩以答其君。至是，蓋曰：公尸言將使爾有子孫者，先當使爾被天祿，而為天命之所附屬焉。其必俾吾君之永膺乎曆數，萬有千歲，綿綿不絕，而非月日之可期；其必俾吾君之永受乎天祿，於萬斯年，勿替引之，而非歲時之可計。惟曆數之永膺，則假哉天命，降于冥冥之中，以附集吾君者，亦萬年而無替，寧有一時之暫離乎？惟天祿之永受，則有命自天，運于蒼蒼之表，以附屬吾君者，亦萬年而無已，寧有一時之暫舍乎？夫以天命而附集於萬年之永，則所謂錫之以胤者，蓋非一朝一夕之故矣。

吁！周之父兄，亦可謂善於祝頌者歟！抑考其詩，此章既曰「景命有僕」，下章申所謂僕者，則曰「釐爾女士，從以孫子」。蓋言天命之所附屬，不過予爾以賢女，使為之妃，又隨之生賢子孫焉耳。合《行葦》而觀之，則周王頌禱於父兄，與父兄祝頌於周王者，
translation_en:
…such enduring length: this is the foundation for the bestowal of descendants. The poet recounts the sacrificial blessing and thus blesses his ruler—how profound his loyalty and affection! In the flourishing days of Zhou, the elders of the ruling lineage, having enjoyed the banquet described in “Thick-Growing Reeds” (Xing Wei), composed this poem in response to their ruler. At this point, its meaning is this: when the ancestral impersonator says that he will grant you sons and grandsons, he must first cause you to receive Heaven’s blessings and become the one to whom Heaven’s Mandate adheres. Surely he will cause our ruler forever to enjoy his allotted span of rule, for ten thousand and a thousand years, continuing without interruption, its limit beyond reckoning in months and days. Surely he will cause our ruler forever to receive Heaven’s blessings, prolonging them without decline for myriad years, beyond reckoning in years and seasons. Only through his enduring enjoyment of that allotted span does the great Mandate of Heaven, descending from the unseen realm to settle upon our ruler, likewise remain undiminished for ten thousand years. Could it ever depart, even momentarily? Only through his enduring reception of Heaven’s blessings does the Mandate from Heaven, moving beyond the blue vault above to attach itself to our ruler, likewise continue without end for ten thousand years. Could it ever leave him, even momentarily? Since Heaven’s Mandate thus settles upon him for the enduring span of ten thousand years, what is called the bestowal of descendants is surely no matter of a single morning or evening.

Ah! May not the elders of Zhou indeed be called skilled in offering blessings and praise? Yet, on examining the poem, we find that this stanza says, “The great Mandate adheres to you,” while the next stanza expands on the meaning of “adheres,” saying, “He bestows upon you a worthy lady, followed by sons and grandsons.” This means simply that Heaven’s Mandate attaches itself to you by granting you a worthy woman to be your consort, and then causing worthy sons and grandsons to be born. Read together with “Thick-Growing Reeds,” the Zhou king’s praises and prayers for his elders, and the elders’ blessings and praises for the Zhou king…

text:
謂夫昔者上帝之命眷我武德之湯何天之龍
治封域於四方何天之休正疆境於四海由是
四方之諸侯無不服我商而受命九州之土地
無不為我商所奄有商有天下實始於此惟我
商之先王歷世受命既不危殆矣故今武丁孫
子嗣守天位猶賴其福焉武丁孫子果何如哉
襲湯號而其武無所不勝稱武王而其德靡有
所愧是以諸侯無不建龍旂之十乘而來覲於
王畿奉黍稷之惟馨而助祭於祖廟王畿之內

…It tells how, in former times, the Supreme Lord’s mandate favored our Tang of martial virtue. Receiving Heaven’s favor, he ordered the territories in all four directions; receiving Heaven’s blessings, he established the boundaries throughout the realm. Thus none of the feudal lords in the four directions failed to submit to our Shang and receive its commands, and none of the lands of the Nine Provinces lay outside our Shang’s possession. Shang’s possession of All under Heaven truly began here. The former kings of our Shang received the mandate through successive generations and were secure from peril. Thus now the descendants of Wu Ding, succeeding to and preserving the heavenly throne, still benefit from their blessings. What, indeed, are these descendants of Wu Ding like? They inherit Tang’s designation, and their martial might prevails everywhere; they bear the title “Martial King,” and their virtue gives them no cause for shame. Thus the feudal lords all raise dragon banners over their ten chariots and come to the royal domain for audience, presenting fragrant millet of both kinds and assisting with sacrifices in the ancestral temple.

The territories, in their breadth, reach to the Four Seas, all of them lands governed by the house of Shang. Thus those who arrive in multitudes from west and east all gaze up at the towering Jing Mountain and cherish a disposition to submit; those who arrive in multitudes from south and north all behold the great river surrounding the land and conceive the wish to attend court and pay homage. Among rites, none is weightier than sacrifice; and in sacrifice, nothing is weightier than winning the people's hearts so that they assist in the observance. 既東齊桓主霸或討罪而恤鄰或存亡而繼絕
名雖是而義則非也有如衛立子頹義所當討
桓則奉王命以討之魯有內難義所當恤桓則
遣高子以省之其伐衛也數之以王命以聲立
頹之罪跡則是矣然罪不可縱而敢縱賂不可
受而遽受奉命之不終其如大義何其來魯也
將南陽之甲以定僖公之位事則美矣然兼圖
廣地之謀窺覘虛實之計來意之不誠其如大
===
義何故春秋於伐衛則貶爵而書人於高子則
不稱使非所以畧其功乎若夫衛被狄難野處
於漕公則城楚丘以封之淮夷不道肆毒於杞
公則城緣陵以遷之城楚丘也從簡書之義使

punctuated: 義如此，《春秋》安得不畧其功以正義哉？昔周室既東，齊桓主霸，或討罪而恤鄰，或存亡而繼絕，名雖是而義則非也。有如衛立子頹，義所當討，桓則奉王命以討之；魯有內難，義所當恤，桓則遣高子以省之。其伐衛也，數之以王命，以聲立頹之罪，跡則是矣。然罪不可縱而敢縱，賂不可受而遽受，奉命之不終，其如大義何？其來魯也，將南陽之甲，以定僖公之位，事則美矣。然兼圖廣地之謀、窺覘虛實之計，來意之不誠，其如大義何？故《春秋》於伐衛則貶爵而書人，於高子則不稱使，非所以畧其功乎？若夫衛被狄難，野處於漕，公則城楚丘以封之；淮夷不道，肆毒於杞，公則城緣陵以遷之。城楚丘也，從簡書之義，使衛之宗社既危而復安，功則偉矣。然策命不作於內史，擯相不掌於宗伯，於義可乎？城緣陵也，致安攘之勞，使杞之人民將亡而復存，績則著矣。然不禀命於王朝，遂專封於下國，於義得乎？故《春秋》於楚丘則沒諸侯而不書，於緣陵則書
translation_en:
…righteousness in this manner [?], how could the Spring and Autumn Annals fail to pass over his achievements in order to uphold righteousness? After the Zhou royal house moved east, Duke Huan of Qi became hegemon. He sometimes punished wrongdoing and aided neighboring states, and sometimes preserved endangered states and restored broken lines of succession. Though these undertakings were right in name, they were wrong in righteousness. For example, when Wei enthroned Zitui, righteousness required punishment, and Duke Huan acted upon the king’s command to attack it. When Lu suffered internal turmoil, righteousness required assistance, and Duke Huan dispatched Gaozi to attend to it. In attacking Wei, he invoked the king’s command to rebuke it and proclaim its crime of enthroning Zitui: outwardly, this was right. Yet he dared let wrongdoing go unpunished when it could not be condoned, and readily accepted bribes that he ought not to have accepted. Having failed to carry out his commission to the end, how did he measure up to the great demands of righteousness? When his forces came to Lu, they brought armored troops from Nanyang to secure Duke Xi’s position: the deed was admirable. Yet their purpose also included schemes to enlarge their territory and to spy out Lu’s strengths and weaknesses. With such insincerity in coming, how did he measure up to the great demands of righteousness? Thus, in recording the attack on Wei, the Spring and Autumn Annals lowers his rank by calling him merely a “man”; in recording Gaozi, it does not say that he was “sent.” Is this not how it passes over his achievements?

When Wei suffered an invasion by the Di and its people lived in the open at Cao, the duke fortified Chuqiu to establish them there. When the Huai Yi acted lawlessly and inflicted harm upon Qi 杞, the duke fortified Yuanling to relocate its people there. In fortifying Chuqiu, he followed the righteous obligation expressed in written summonses to mutual aid, restoring security to Wei’s ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain after they had been imperiled. His achievement was indeed great. Yet the investiture document was not prepared by the Interior Scribe, nor were the ceremonial proceedings directed by the Minister of Rites. Was this permissible according to righteousness? In fortifying Yuanling, he labored to bring peace and repel aggressors, preserving the people of Qi when they were on the verge of destruction. His accomplishment was indeed conspicuous. Yet he did not receive authorization from the royal court, but presumed to establish a fief among the subordinate states on his own authority. Was this consonant with righteousness? Thus, for Chuqiu, the Spring and Autumn Annals suppresses mention of the feudal lords and does not record them; for Yuanling, it records…

translation_en:
…the regional lords, but does not list them in order. Is this not likewise a means of discounting his achievements? In general, the method of the Spring and Autumn Annals is to uphold righteousness without seeking advantage, to make the Way manifest without reckoning achievements, and to pass over minor kindnesses while preserving the great principles of conduct. It simply judges people by what is right. As for Duke Huan of Qi, his achievements and the benefits he brought certainly surpassed those of his contemporaries; but measured against the Way and righteousness, how could his conduct have been entirely correct? He was indeed an offender against the Three Kings. Alas! Is this why Confucian scholars are ashamed to speak of him?
“The men of Chu attacked Xu. The duke met with the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Zheng, the Baron of Xu 許, and the Earl of Cao to covenant at Muqiu; they then encamped at Kuang. Gongsun Ao led an army and joined the great officers of the regional lords in relieving Xu 徐.” 〔All from the fifteenth year of Duke Xi.〕
Bao Nan
Comment by Associate Examiner Tong, School Instructor: Among treatments of this topic capable of giving some satisfaction, this essay alone was found, like gold picked out by sifting sand. Its writing is imposing and disciplined, its diction and tone mature and antique. It should be recorded to instruct future students.
Comment by Examiner Li, Expositor: It grasps the original intent of Hu’s Commentary.
Comment by Examiner Luo, Vice Director of the Library: The handling of the topic is methodical; the censure and commendation at the end are appropriate.
Men from afar raised an army to oppress a small state, while the hegemon failed in his duty to succor those in distress. The Spring and Autumn Annals records the events in full to censure them. Here the men of Chu attacked Xu, but Duke Huan failed to relieve it effectively. The Annals records the attack, the covenant, the encampment, and the relief: what is the intention behind its censure? Now Xu, as a state, had abandoned the barbarians and joined the civilized realm; though small, it had attached itself to a great power. Moreover, Qi and Chu were enemies…

title: 成化十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
也當夫楚人懷取舒之憾涉江淮之險而肆彼
狼貪越陳蔡之遠而逞其蠶食雖曰虐徐之國
也而實以震齊之鄰雖曰掠徐之疆也而實欲
造齊之鄙蓋其為謀也深而其為罪也大矣齊
桓者以天子之命侯為中國之盟主以封境言
則關唇亡齒寒之慮有當救之義以形勢言則
無餽糧越險之難有可救之理攘夷安夏此其
時也極焚援溺容可緩乎胡乃先會牡丘以為
尋盟之舉繼次于匡以為頓兵之計而但遣列
===
國之大夫為三軍之主將以從事焉名曰攘楚
也未嘗為必勝之圖名曰救徐也曽何有實惠
之及蓋不惟失徐之望而亦以失天下之望不
惟損齊之威而亦以損中國之威矣恤患之義
固當如是邪故春秋書楚人伐徐則其暴橫憑
凌之罪著矣書盟于牡丘見諸侯救患之不協
矣書次于匡見霸主號令之不嚴矣書大夫帥
師而諸侯不行見桓德益衰而攘夷狄安中國
之志怠矣夫以一徐之利害而荊楚之強弱繫

也當夫楚人懷取舒之憾涉江淮之險而肆彼
狼貪越陳蔡之遠而逞其蠶食雖曰居徐之國
也而實以震齊之鄰雖曰掠徐之疆也而實欲
造齊之郤蓋其爲謀也深而其爲罪也大矣齊
桓者以天子之命做爲中國之盟主以封疆言
則關唇亡齒寒之慮有當救之義以形勢言則
無餽糧越險之難有可救之理攘夷安夏此其
時也拯焚援溺容可緩乎胡乃先會牡丘以爲
尋盟之舉繼次于匡以爲觀兵之計而但遣列
===
國之大夫爲三軍之主將以從事焉名曰攘楚
也未嘗爲必勝之圖名曰救徐也曾何有實惠
之及蓋不惟失徐之望而亦以失天下之望不
惟損齊之威而亦以損中國之威矣攄患之義
固當如是邪故春秋書楚人伐徐則其恣横憑
凌之罪著矣書盟于牡丘見諸侯救患之不協
矣書次于匡見霸主號令之不嚴矣書大夫帥
師而諸侯不行見桓德益衰而攘夷狄安中國
之志怠矣夫以一徐之利害而荆楚之强弱繫
punctuated: 也。當夫楚人懷取舒之憾，涉江淮之險而肆彼狼貪，越陳蔡之遠而逞其蠶食，雖曰虐徐之國也，而實以震齊之鄰；雖曰掠徐之疆也，而實欲造齊之鄙。蓋其為謀也深，而其為罪也大矣。齊桓者，以天子之命侯，為中國之盟主。以封境言，則關唇亡齒寒之慮，有當救之義；以形勢言，則無餽糧越險之難，有可救之理。攘夷安夏，此其時也。極焚援溺，容可緩乎？胡乃先會牡丘，以為尋盟之舉，繼次于匡，以為頓兵之計，而但遣列國之大夫為三軍之主將，以從事焉？名曰攘楚也，未嘗為必勝之圖；名曰救徐也，曽何有實惠之及？蓋不惟失徐之望，而亦以失天下之望；不惟損齊之威，而亦以損中國之威矣。恤患之義，固當如是邪？故《春秋》書「楚人伐徐」，則其暴橫憑凌之罪著矣；書「盟于牡丘」，見諸侯救患之不協矣；書「次于匡」，見霸主號令之不嚴矣；書大夫帥師而諸侯不行，見桓德益衰，而攘夷狄、安中國之志怠矣。夫以一徐之利害，而荊楚之強弱繫
translation_en:
…were enemies. When the men of Chu, nursing resentment over the capture of Shu, crossed the perilous Yangzi and Huai rivers to indulge their wolfish greed, and passed beyond distant Chen and Cai to pursue their gradual encroachments, they ostensibly sought to ravage the state of Xu, but in reality meant to intimidate Qi’s neighbors. They ostensibly sought to plunder Xu’s territory, but in reality wished to reach Qi’s borders. Their designs were indeed far-reaching, and their offense grave.

Duke Huan of Qi, a lord appointed by the Son of Heaven, was leader of the covenant among the central states. In terms of territorial boundaries, he faced the danger expressed in the saying, “When the lips are lost, the teeth grow cold,” and therefore had a duty to rescue Xu. In terms of strategic circumstances, he faced no difficulty in transporting provisions across dangerous terrain, and therefore had the means to rescue it. This was the moment to repel the barbarians and secure the Xia states. Could rescuing those in flames [?] and drawing out the drowning permit delay? Why, then, did he first assemble at Muqiu to renew the covenant, next encamp at Kuang as a measure for holding his troops in place, and merely dispatch the grandees of the various states as commanders of the armies to undertake the operation? In name, he was repelling Chu, yet he never devised a plan to ensure victory. In name, he was rescuing Xu, yet what tangible benefit ever reached it? He disappointed not only Xu’s hopes but also those of all under Heaven; he diminished not only Qi’s prestige but also that of the central states. Was this truly how the duty of relieving distress ought to be fulfilled?

Thus, when the Spring and Autumn Annals records, “The men of Chu attacked Xu,” their offense of violent aggression and bullying is made manifest. When it records, “They covenanted at Muqiu,” it reveals the lords’ lack of unity in relieving distress. When it records, “They encamped at Kuang,” it reveals the hegemon’s lack of rigor in issuing commands. When it records that the grandees led the armies while the lords themselves did not go, it reveals that Duke Huan’s virtue had declined further, and that his resolve to repel the Yi and Di barbarians and secure the central states had grown slack. Now, upon the fortunes of Xu alone, the strength or weakness of Jing-Chu depended…

title: 成化十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
歟齊霸之盛衰關焉此聖人所以反覆而加之
意也歟吁自召陵之後桓霸漸衰楚力寢強伐
國必書皆以累齊桓也而於此尤致詳焉楚之
惡固不待言矣霸主之任其責也亦豈聖人之
得已哉然終桓之世楚不書爵則桓之功在當
時亦不可誣也
禮記
禮之以多為貴者以其外心者也德發揚
詡萬物大理物博如此則得不以多為貴
===
乎故君子樂其發也禮之以少為貴者以
其內心也德產之致也精微觀天下之物
無可以稱其德者如此則得不以少為貴
乎是故君子慎其獨也
王弘

歟？齊霸之盛衰關焉，此聖人所以反覆而加之意也歟？吁！自召陵之後，桓霸漸衰，楚力寢強，伐國必書，皆以累齊桓也，而於此尤致詳焉。楚之惡固不待言矣，霸主之任其責也，亦豈聖人之得已哉？然終桓之世，楚不書爵，則桓之功在當時亦不可誣也。

禮記

禮之以多為貴者，以其外心者也。德發揚，詡萬物，大理物博，如此則得不以多為貴乎？故君子樂其發也。禮之以少為貴者，以其內心也。德產之致也精微，觀天下之物，無可以稱其德者，如此則得不以少為貴乎？是故君子慎其獨也。

王弘

translation_en:
…? The flourishing or decline of Qi’s hegemony was bound up with this. Was this why the Sage returned to the matter repeatedly and gave it such attention? Alas! After Shaoling, Duke Huan’s hegemony gradually declined, while Chu’s power steadily increased. Every attack upon another state was recorded, each bringing discredit upon Duke Huan of Qi; here the account is especially detailed. Chu’s wickedness surely needs no explanation. Yet could the Sage have avoided holding the hegemonic lord responsible? Nevertheless, throughout Duke Huan’s lifetime, Chu’s ruler was never recorded with his noble title. Thus Huan’s achievements in his own time cannot be denied either.

Record of Rites

“Where ritual prizes abundance, it does so because the mind is directed outward. Virtue spreads forth, nurturing the myriad things; its ordering is vast and the things it embraces numerous. This being so, how could abundance fail to be prized? Thus the gentleman delights in its outward expression. Where ritual prizes spareness, it does so because the mind is directed inward. The ultimate workings by which virtue brings things forth are subtle and minute. Looking upon all the things under Heaven, none can match that virtue. This being so, how could spareness fail to be prized? Thus the gentleman is watchful over himself when alone.”

Wang Hong

Comment by Examiner Li, Expositor: “Tracing the outward and inward to their underlying unity is most apt.”

title: 成化十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
禮貴於備物必原其所以貴乎物禮貴於存誠
必原其所以貴乎誠夫大祭之禮所貴不同由
聖人所見於造化者不同也記者於此不得不兩
原其意而申言之哉且夫祭天饗地禮之大者
也是禮也有品具水陸物兼陰陽而以多為貴
者豈以美沒禮哉以其主於備物而外用其心
焉耳何也聖人盖見夫天地之德發揚昭著盛
大溥徧於萬物是其理之所該者大故其物之
所成者博如此不大其報弗稱也得不貴於多
===
乎此制禮君子所以樂其用心於外以致備物
之饗貴其多而不以為侈焉是禮也有特牲是
尚明水是薦而以少為貴者豈以菲廢禮哉以
其主於存誠而內用其心焉耳何也聖人盖見
夫天地之德所以發生萬彙者其流行賦予之
理密緻而精微縱使徧取天下之物終難以為
功德之報如此雖極其備弗稱也得不貴於少
乎是以行禮君子唯謹其一念之微以致夫神
明之交貴其少而不以為儉焉吁始也以天地

translation_en: When ritual values the completeness of offerings, one must trace why it values material things; when ritual values preserving sincerity, one must trace why it values sincerity. That the rites of great sacrifices value different things arises from the different aspects of the workings of creation that the sages perceived. Could the recorder here fail to investigate both intentions and elaborate upon them? Now, sacrificing to Heaven and presenting offerings to Earth are the greatest rites. In these rites, some value abundance, with a full assortment of products from water and land and offerings encompassing both yin and yang. Could this mean allowing sumptuousness to overwhelm ritual? It is simply because they focus on providing complete offerings and direct the mind outward. Why is this? The sages perceived that the virtue of Heaven and Earth manifests itself clearly and conspicuously, vast and abundant, extending everywhere throughout the myriad things. Its principle embraces so much that the things it brings to completion are correspondingly manifold. In this case, without a magnificent act of recompense, the return would be inadequate. How could abundance fail to be valued? This is why the gentlemen who established ritual gladly directed their minds outward to present a full array of offerings, valuing their abundance without considering it extravagance. In these same rites, some value sparseness, esteeming a single sacrificial animal and presenting bright water. Could this mean allowing meagreness to abolish ritual? It is simply because they focus on preserving sincerity and direct the mind inward. Why is this? The sages perceived that, in the virtue of Heaven and Earth that generates the myriad kinds of things, the principle that circulates and bestows is intricate and exceedingly subtle. Even if one gathered things from throughout the world, they would ultimately be insufficient to repay its achievements and beneficence. In this case, even the fullest provision would be inadequate. How could sparseness fail to be valued? Thus the gentlemen who perform ritual attend carefully to the subtlest stirrings of a single thought, thereby achieving communion with the spirits, valuing sparseness without considering it parsimony. Ah! At first, on account of Heaven and Earth …

title: 成化十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
之德之大而禮以外心為敬終也以天地之德

…the greatness of the virtue of Heaven and Earth, ritual expresses reverence by directing the heart outward; ultimately, because of the subtlety of the virtue of Heaven and Earth, ritual expresses reverence by directing the heart inward. Whether outward or inward, is not the aim always to make the observance fitting? In general, the way of sacrifice takes sincerity as its foundation and material offerings as its means. Those who fully realize sincerity within will assuredly provide complete offerings; those who merely provide complete offerings may not have fully realized sincerity. If a sacrifice lacks sincerity, the spirits will assuredly not accept it. What benefit, then, is there in sacrificing? The Book of Documents says: “It is not millet that gives fragrance; illustrious virtue alone gives fragrance.” The Book of Changes says: “The eastern neighbor slaughters an ox, but does not equal the western neighbor who performs the modest yue sacrifice and truly receives its blessing.” Viewed in light of this [?], the subtle intent underlying the sages’ deliberations on ritual can be discerned.

向非君子致其道以自治而有得焉曷克以臻

和則一心之天無非樂矣是以天神渾融燁然

translation_en:
…others. Indeed, the effects of ritual and music are abundantly manifest in one's person and profoundly move others. Had the gentleman not fully realized their Way in governing himself and thereby attained something within, how could he have reached this state? The Record of Music means that when the gentleman brings music to its fullest realization to govern his heart and perfect its harmony, the Heaven-given nature of his heart is wholly musical. Thus his Heaven-given spirit [?] is thoroughly integrated, and the radiance of virtue shines and stirs within; harmony and compliance fill him, and their rich flowering appears without. The manifestation of music is entirely spontaneous. How could he initially have intended that the people obey him? Yet throughout all under Heaven, shaped by the transforming influence of great music, everyone comes together in harmony: restless hearts are calmed and desires released. They honor him and obey his commands, and not a single person remains violent or unruly. This is what is meant by “Perfect music has no sound, yet all under Heaven is harmonious.” Why speak merely of “looking upon his countenance and not contending with him”?

When he brings ritual to its fullest realization to govern his person and perfect its compliance, every function of his body accords with ritual. Thus every movement of his bearing conforms to proper measure, and every turn conforms to ritual. The [illegible] of ritual, too, is spontaneous. How could he initially have intended that the people submit to him? Yet everywhere within the land's bounds, encompassed by the transforming influence of great ritual, everyone becomes docile: reverence arises in their hearts and arrogance is checked. They respectfully receive and follow his orders, and not a single person remains defiant or disobedient. This is what is meant by “Perfect ritual requires no yielding, yet all under Heaven is well governed.” Why speak merely of “looking upon his appearance and feeling no disrespect or arrogance”? That the people are moved by me in this way is likewise entirely spontaneous. Are not the effects of ritual and music great indeed? Generally speaking…

text:
各發必一佳上也
觀孝者必於其所自立德而至於聖則其
為孝也大矣人之所自立者孰有大於德
哉人子之所以顯其親者亦孰有大於德
哉聖人德以立其身顯其名以及乎其親
德愈至名愈顯而親愈尊矣天下之孝孰
大於此然則孰能之舜能之孰能言之吾

punctuated:
各發必一佳上也。

觀孝者，必於其所自立。德而至於聖，則其為孝也大矣。人之所自立者，孰有大於德哉？人子之所以顯其親者，亦孰有大於德哉？聖人德以立其身，顯其名以及乎其親。德愈至，名愈顯，而親愈尊矣。天下之孝，孰大於此？然則孰能之？舜能之。孰能言之？吾夫子之言也。「德為聖人」，請言舜所以為孝之大。夫孝亦一德也，以孝言德可也，而曷為以德言孝也？曰：此有所主言之也。人之德非止乎孝，而孝其先也；聖人之德非止乎孝，而益足以見其大也。人之所以有身者，非親乎？人之所以為人者，非以其德乎？惟不知以德事其親也，於是有欲貴其親者，有欲富其親者，有欲其親之名與壽者。是可以為孝乎？曰：此孝之小者也，非聖人之所謂孝也。聖人之所謂孝者，德也。今以一藝自立者，謂之才，人則稱之曰：「是才子」
translation_en:
…each expression is invariably excellent [?].

To assess filial piety, one must look to that by which a person establishes himself. If his virtue reaches sagehood, his filial piety is indeed great. Among the means by which a person establishes himself, what is greater than virtue? Among the means by which a son brings distinction to his parents, what likewise is greater than virtue? Through virtue, the sage establishes himself and makes his name illustrious, extending that distinction to his parents. The more consummate his virtue, the more illustrious his name and the more honored his parents. What filial piety in the world is greater than this? Who, then, could accomplish it? Shun could. Who could express it? These are the words of our Master: “In virtue, he was a sage.” Allow me to explain why Shun’s filial piety was great.

Filial piety is itself a virtue. It is appropriate to discuss virtue in terms of filial piety; why, then, discuss filial piety in terms of virtue? I reply: this statement has a particular focus. Human virtue is not confined to filial piety, but filial piety comes first. The sage’s virtue is not confined to filial piety, yet it makes the greatness of his filial piety all the more apparent. Is it not from their parents that people receive their bodies? Is it not through virtue that people are human? It is only because people do not understand how to serve their parents through virtue that some wish to make their parents noble, some wish to make them wealthy, and some wish for their parents to enjoy renown and longevity. Can this count as filial piety? I reply: this is filial piety in its lesser form, not what the sage calls filial piety. What the sage calls filial piety is virtue. Now, someone who establishes himself through a single skill is considered talented, and people praise him, saying: “This is a talented son …”

行之不備集天下之才以爲才無一藝之
不周非聖人而能若是乎夫聖也者人之
至者也天下之所取法焉者也耕于歷山
===
漁于雷澤陶于河濱山澤之人皆知之曰
是聖人也所居成聚二年成邑三年成都
都邑之人皆知之曰是聖人也愼徽五典
而五典克從納于百揆而百揆時敘賓于
四門而四門穆穆天下之人皆知之曰是
聖人也夫以一人之身居于天下之大而
天下稱之爲聖聖非聖人而能若是乎蓋
不惟知其爲聖人也且從而稱其鄉曰此
聖人之鄉也稱其譽曰此聖人之族也稱
punctuated: 也」，尚足以顯其親，而况德乎？以一行自立者，謂之賢人，則稱之曰：「是賢子也。」尚足以顯其親，而况德之至者乎？舜之德何德也？濬哲而文明，溫恭而允塞，明於庶物，察於人倫，德之生知者也；由仁義行，非行仁義，德之安行者也。合天下之善以為善，無一行之不備；集天下之才以為才，無一藝之不周。非聖人而能若是乎？夫聖也者，人之至者也，天下之所取法焉者也。耕于歷山，漁于雷澤，陶于河濱，山澤之人皆知之，曰：「是聖人也。」所居成聚，二年成邑，三年成都，都邑之人皆知之，曰：「是聖人也。」愼徽五典，而五典克從；納于百揆，而百揆時敍；賓于四門，而四門穆穆。天下之人皆知之，曰：「是聖人也。」夫以一人之身，居乎天下之大，而天下稱之無異辭，非聖人而能若是乎？蓋不惟知其為聖人也，又從而稱其鄉，曰：「此聖人之鄉也。」稱其族，曰：「此聖人之族也。」稱
translation_en: …Such a person can still bring honor to his parents; how much more so one possessed of virtue! Someone who establishes himself through a single form of good conduct is called a worthy man, and people say of him, “This is a worthy son.” He can still bring honor to his parents; how much more so one whose virtue is consummate! What sort of virtue did Shun possess? Profoundly wise and radiantly accomplished, gentle and reverent, sincere and steadfast, he understood the myriad things and discerned human relationships: his knowledge of virtue was innate. He acted from benevolence and righteousness, rather than merely putting benevolence and righteousness into practice: he practiced virtue with natural ease. He embraced all the goodness under Heaven as his own goodness, lacking no form of good conduct; he gathered all the abilities under Heaven as his own abilities, lacking proficiency in no skill. Could anyone but a sage be like this? A sage is the highest perfection of humanity, one whom all under Heaven take as their model. When he plowed at Lishan, fished at Leize, and made pottery on the riverbank, the people of the hills and marshes all recognized him and said, “This is a sage.” Wherever he settled became a community; in two years it became a town, and in three years a city. The people of the cities and towns all recognized him and said, “This is a sage.” He carefully brought distinction to the five teachings, and the five teachings were duly observed; he was appointed to oversee the hundred affairs, and the hundred affairs were put in proper order; he received guests at the four gates, and at the four gates all was harmonious and reverent. All the people under Heaven recognized him and said, “This is a sage.” For a single person living amid the vastness of the world to receive its unanimous praise—could anyone but a sage achieve this? Indeed, people not only recognized him as a sage, but went on to praise his native place, saying, “This is the native place of a sage.” They praised his clan, saying, “This is the clan of a sage.” They praised …

其親曰此聖人之所自出也夫使其身為
聖人而其父為聖人之父聖人之為孝何
如哉居天子之尊而尊其親為天子之父
尊之至也有四海之富而奉其親以四海
之養養之至也上而宗廟饗其祀則由其
親以至於祖考其隆也孰加焉下而子孫
保其業則由其親以及於後世其遠也孰
加焉噫聖人之孝其大一至此哉或者乃
曰夫所謂富貴名壽者孝之小者也而聖

名壽萃焉聖人之孝之大何如哉或者又

至必待是以為孝則人之為孝亦難矣吾

translation_en:
…of his parent, they say: “This is the one from whom the sage sprang.” When he himself becomes a sage, and his father thereby becomes the father of a sage, how great is the sage’s filial piety! Occupying the exalted position of Son of Heaven, he honors his parent as the father of the Son of Heaven: this is the utmost honor. Possessing the wealth of all within the Four Seas, he supports his parent with the resources of all within the Four Seas: this is the utmost provision. Above, in the ancestral temples, his forebears receive his sacrificial offerings, extending from his parent back to his ancestors: what could surpass this in grandeur? Below, his descendants preserve his patrimony, extending from his parent onward to later generations: what could surpass this in lasting reach? Ah! Can the greatness of the sage’s filial piety reach such heights!
Someone then asks: “Wealth, noble standing, renown, and longevity are minor aspects of filial piety. Why, then, does the sage practice filial piety through these?” The reply is: “What are called the sage’s emoluments, rank, renown, and longevity are all brought about by virtue; they are not acquired by mere chance. When virtue flourishes in his person, emoluments, rank, renown, and longevity come to him. When his virtue extends to his parent, these blessings gather upon his parent. How great is the sage’s filial piety!”
Someone further asks: “Virtue resides in human beings, while emoluments, rank, renown, and longevity depend upon Heaven. What resides in human beings can be attained through effort; what depends upon Heaven cannot be certain to arrive. If one must await these things before being filial, then practicing filial piety is indeed difficult. Yet our Master held that, in Shun’s case, these were things that great virtue must assuredly obtain. Why is this?” The reply is: “Heaven and humanity share a single principle. The sage’s virtue is virtue at its utmost. Heaven…”

道福善理之至者也事事而求之屑屑而
論之若有不同及其至則未有不合者也
聖人豈有心於祿位名壽之間哉觀人之
所必歸與天之所必應則聖人之孝之大
益可見矣豈可以天下之所謂德所謂孝
者槩論之哉子思子作中庸引此以明道
之費此可與知道者言也抑夫子嘗以孝

道福善，理之至者也。事事而求之，屑屑而論之，若有不同；及其至，則未有不合者也。聖人豈有心於祿位名壽之間哉？觀人之所必歸與天之所必應，則聖人之孝之大益可見矣。豈可以天下之所謂德、所謂孝者槩論之哉？子思子作《中庸》，引此以明道之費，此可與知道者言也。抑夫子嘗以孝稱武王矣，蓋其所得於天者皆同，獨不稱其德而稱其名，稱其達而不稱其大。武王獨非聖人哉？於是見舜之德，雖武王不能以同也。武王且不能同，況後世乎？況天下之所謂德、所謂孝者乎？然則德為聖人，而得祿位名壽於天如舜者，幸復見聖天子于今日。
