translation_en:
…the Way of Heaven blesses the good: this is principle at its utmost. If one examines matters individually and discusses them in minute detail, they may seem to differ; yet at their utmost, they never fail to accord. Would a sage deliberately concern himself with emolument, rank, renown, and longevity? When we observe where people inevitably turn their allegiance and what Heaven inevitably answers, the greatness of the sage’s filial piety becomes still more apparent. How could it be judged indiscriminately alongside what the world calls virtue and filial piety? When Master Zisi composed the Doctrine of the Mean, he cited this to illuminate the all-pervading scope of the Way. This can be discussed with those who understand the Way.

Yet the Master once praised King Wu for his filial piety. What he received from Heaven was, indeed, the same; nevertheless, the Master praised his renown rather than his virtue, and the universally acknowledged character of his filial piety rather than its greatness. Was King Wu alone not a sage? Here we see that even King Wu could not equal Shun’s virtue. If even King Wu could not equal it, how much less could later generations? How much less could what the world calls virtue and filial piety? Thus, one whose virtue makes him a sage and who receives emolument, rank, renown, and longevity from Heaven, as Shun did—we are fortunate to behold such a one again today in our sagely Son of Heaven.

Seated in embroidered robes upon the throne, you have the dance of shields and plumes performed on the steps of Shun’s court; hearing affairs of government in the Hall of Light, you have proclamations displayed on the gate towers of Zhou’s palace. …in this enlightened age. We completed the rites on the day of the offering of vegetables to the Sage and entered our names on the court rolls on the day we proceeded to court. From the highest councils of government downward, all have witnessed this, declaring that never since the establishment of the examination system has its splendor been greater.

Your servant humbly reflects that the first-ranked Palace Examination graduate represents the finest selection in literary accomplishment, and that becoming a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) is indeed the proper path for men of outstanding ability. We, your servants, possess inferior talents, like humble turnips and radishes, and offer the insignificant opinions of grass-cutters and wood-gatherers. Searching through chapters and picking out phrases, how could we escape the charge of touching upon one thing while overlooking ten thousand? Through your inclusive acceptance, we have fortunately been numbered among those selected—even though, of ten chosen, only five may prove worthy. How could we dare fail to emulate the resolve to be last to enjoy ease and first to bear concern, pledging together to rise early and retire late? Our hearts are at one with Zheng Xie 鄭爕, fearing that we cannot meet the demand for loyalty and filial devotion; in our learning we aspire to Wang Zeng 王曾, wishing never to forget his admonition concerning warmth and a full belly. Third Session. Policy Essay. First Question.

Gong Qin.

Comment by Associate Examiner Fan, Assistant Instructor: This essay fully recounts the greatness of the Sagely Progenitor’s founding enterprise and the dynastic succession he established, far surpassing those of earlier dynasties. Its author is a man of discernment.

Moreover, its language is expansive, seemingly inexhaustible. It truly merits the high recommendation received in the preceding sessions. How could it be unworthy?

Comment by Examiner Li, Expositor: Reading through this policy essay amply demonstrates how profoundly the men educated and nurtured by our dynasty have absorbed its transforming influence.

Comment by Examiner Luo, Editorial Director: The first question was intended precisely to see how the candidates had studied and recited accounts of our sagely and enlightened sovereign’s abundant virtue and great achievements. This essay is powerful, comprehensive, and detailed; it should be recorded and shown to students.

text:

太祖高皇帝創業之大也猗歟盛哉

甲有丕顯之文王丕承之武王而後有嗣

translation_en:
…the maxims of the instructional canons, heard the elders’ praises and discussions, and looked up in admiration! Considering antiquity, how great was the founding achievement of Taizu, the Exalted Emperor! Ah, how magnificent! Only after Yu, who possessed statutes and rules, came Qi, who could reverently carry on his succession. Only after Tang, who first established the proper ordering of human relationships, came Tai Jia, who inherited his admirable legacy. Only after the greatly illustrious King Wen and King Wu, who grandly continued his work, came Kings Cheng and Kang, who inherited and upheld the great instructions and followed the great laws. By examining what the founders established, one can understand what their successors preserved.

As for Emperor Gao of Han’s pacification of the realm, the histories praise the grandeur and far-reaching scope of his plans. Yet rites and music were not instituted, the well-field system was not restored, the prohibition on possessing books was not abolished, and the myriad particulars of government remained unaddressed. Thus his successors all mingled the methods of hegemonic rule into their institutions. As for Taizong of Tang’s pacification of the realm, the histories praise the brilliance of his institutions and precedents. Yet instruction in the constant moral relationships was not pure, the distinction between non-Chinese peoples and the Chinese was not properly maintained, and the schools were not fully established. The fundamental principles were not correctly set, and so his successors likewise mingled non-Chinese practices into their government. As for Taizu of Song’s pacification of the realm, the histories praise his many reforms of the defective policies of the Five Dynasties. Yet the lands of Ling and Xia were not recovered, the territories of You and Yan were not restored, and military prowess was insufficient. Consequently, his successors were left with enduring regret over the Central Plain.

When the founding has been imperfect, it is indeed difficult to demand that its preservation be complete. Is this not why the founding achievement of our Exalted Emperor was so great? For, with…

天所全予之大德，成開闢以來所未有之大功，建億萬載不拔之大業，蕩蕩乎！巍巍乎！不可得而擬議矣。姑舉數者言之：家法之純正，朝政之嚴肅，學校有制，科目有式，祭祀有名義，禮儀有節目，刑法有律令，而軍旅有紀綱，以至於居室冠服之制、聲音文字之書、農工商賈之業，凡聖賢所行、書契所載，莫不斟之酌之，與時宜之，合之乎衆理之中，斷之以聖心之一。内外本末兼舉而無遺，巨細精粗並存而不闕，誠如執事所謂集帝王之大成者矣。

translation_en:
…with the great virtue that Heaven bestowed upon him in its fullness, he accomplished great deeds unequalled since the beginning of the world and established a great imperial enterprise that would stand unshaken for countless ages. How boundless! How lofty! It is beyond comparison or description. Let me cite just a few examples: the purity and rectitude of his dynastic household rules; the solemn discipline of court government; established regulations for schools; prescribed forms for the examination categories; proper designations and principles for sacrifices; detailed procedures for ritual observances; statutes and ordinances for criminal justice; and order and discipline for the armed forces. These extended to regulations for dwellings, caps, and clothing; books on sounds and written characters; and the occupations of farmers, artisans, and merchants. Whatever the sages and worthies had practised, and whatever written records contained, he weighed and considered, adapted to the needs of the times, brought into accord with the proper balance of all principles, and decided through the single-minded resolve of his sagely heart. Inner and outer affairs, fundamentals and particulars—all were attended to without omission. Great and small, refined and coarse—all were accommodated without deficiency. Truly, as you have said, he brought together the supreme achievements of emperors and kings.
As for the statement in the Grand Pronouncements (Da gao) that ruler and ministers journey together, this expresses the meaning of their relationship as head and limbs. Its injunction to elucidate the Five Constant Virtues is precisely the teaching of giving due weight to the constant norms and putting ritual propriety into practice. Are not the eighteen matters concerning the ruler’s way in the Comprehensive Instructions for Aiding the World (Zishi tongxun) an expression of the resolve to recognize the difficulties of being a sovereign? Are not its seventeen matters concerning the service of ministers an admonition to those holding office …

translation_en:
…the admonition? Compared with the institutions of the Canons and Counsels, these accord like matching tallies despite belonging to different ages; compared with the texts of the Instructions and Announcements, they follow the same course despite differing in expression. This can scarcely be set forth in just one or two examples. How could the rulers of the Han, Tang, or Song even remotely approach one ten-thousandth of this achievement!
The successive sage emperors have inherited and carried forward the great imperial enterprise. Their spiritual majesty shines brilliantly, manifesting the presence of the sagely founder in Heaven; the Great Way flows onward, splendidly displaying the sagely instructions handed down to the world. His Majesty, with his benevolent and sagely virtue, reigns in an age of preserving established achievements. Even such rulers as Qi, Tai Jia, and Kings Cheng and Kang scarcely merit mention by comparison.
Today, at court and within the government offices, institutions and cultural forms conform solely to established laws, while rites, music, governance, and punishments adhere solely to the enlightened instructions. This is good government for ten thousand generations. All who serve as subjects throughout the realm devote themselves to loyalty and filial piety, never daring to parade their cleverness and thereby disrupt the old statutes. All the common people throughout the realm follow the Way and its paths, none indulging personal likes or dislikes so as to depart from the August Standard. This is moral transformation for ten thousand generations. The great ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain can be preserved as securely as Mount Tai; the vast realm within the seas can be placed on foundations as firm as bedrock. This is an imperial enterprise for ten thousand generations. As for me, in my ignorance …

title: 成化十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
所以拳拳於心學之問而亦愚之所願承
學焉者也愚雖不敏敢不誦所聞以就正
乎夫心者人之神明所以具衆理而應萬
事者也天雖高此心之運可以與之同其
高地雖遠此心之運可以與之同其遠天
地高遠此心既有以同之此人所以能參
天地而為三才者不越乎一心而已昔帝
舜之命禹有曰人心惟危道心惟微蓋以
人莫不有天賦之形心之發由於形氣之
===
私者是為人心亦莫不有天賦之性心之
發由於性命之正者是為道心其初固渾
然在中未嘗判而為二也孟軻氏之示學
者有曰盡心知性存心養性蓋以其能極
此心之全體而無不盡故曰盡心屬知之
事以其能操持此心而無一時之或舍故
曰存心屬行之事知行並進之工夫不可
以先後論也文王小心翼翼者聖人之一
於敬也孔子從心所欲不踰矩者聖人之

translation_en:
…thus the earnest concern with the question of learning concerning the mind-and-heart, a subject in which I too humbly wish to receive instruction. Though I am slow of understanding, dare I fail to recite what I have heard and submit it for correction? The mind-and-heart is the spiritual intelligence of the human being: it embodies the many principles and responds to all affairs. Though Heaven is high, the workings of this mind can match its height; though Earth extends far, the workings of this mind can match its extent. Since this mind can match the height and extent of Heaven and Earth, the reason human beings can stand alongside Heaven and Earth to constitute the Three Powers lies in this mind alone.

When Emperor Shun charged Yu, he said: “The human mind is precarious; the mind of the Way is subtle.” Everyone has a bodily form endowed by Heaven. When the mind’s activity proceeds from the particular interests of bodily form and vital energy, this is the human mind. Everyone likewise has a nature endowed by Heaven. When the mind’s activity proceeds from the rectitude of this nature and Heaven’s mandate, this is the mind of the Way. At their origin, they are an undivided whole within us, never separated into two.

In instructing learners, Meng Ke said: “Fully realize the mind and know the nature; preserve the mind and nourish the nature.” Because one can reach the full compass of this mind, leaving nothing unrealized, this is called fully realizing the mind and belongs to knowing. Because one can hold fast to this mind without letting it go for a single moment, this is called preserving the mind and belongs to acting. The work of advancing in knowing and acting together cannot be discussed as a matter of one preceding the other. text:
純乎理也言之不同者所指之事不同也
以君子之處危地而言故知其日夕之憂
懼以君子之循理而言故知其胸次之寬
廣言之有異者所論之意異也惻隱羞惡
辭讓是非四者皆善端之發見固人所必
有然知之而不能充者私欲間之耳忿懥
恐懼好樂憂患四者皆心之用固人所不
能無然有之即不得其正者欲動情勝耳
大人之心所以同於赤子者通達萬變一
===
純一無僞之本然而已告子之不動心所
以先於孟氏者未嘗知義特强制其心使
之不動而已自一陽之初動觀之故曰以
生物爲心自造化之本然論之故曰無心
而成化此皆程子各有攸當之言也豈自
相背戾邪以明鑑照物言之故曰心有所
主則虛以弊屋禦寇言之故曰心有所主
則實此皆程子各有所指之言也豈故爲
不一邪孟子養心莫善於寡欲之說深有

…being wholly in accord with principle. These statements differ because they refer to different matters. Speaking of the gentleman’s situation amid danger, we recognize his anxiety and apprehension day and night; speaking of his following principle, we recognize the breadth and openness of his heart. The statements differ because their intended meanings differ.

Commiseration, shame and aversion, deference and yielding, and the sense of right and wrong are all manifestations of the beginnings of goodness, which everyone necessarily possesses. If people recognize these but cannot develop them fully, it is merely because selfish desires intervene. Anger, fear, fondness, and anxiety are all activities of the heart, which people cannot be without. Yet when their presence prevents the heart from attaining its proper state, it is merely because desire is aroused and emotion prevails.

The heart of the great person resembles that of an infant because, while comprehending myriad changes, it retains its original condition of purity, unity, and freedom from falsity [?]. Gaozi attained an unmoved heart before Mengzi because, without ever understanding righteousness, he merely forced his heart to remain unmoved.

Viewed from the first stirring of the single yang force, it is therefore said that giving life to things is its heart; considered in terms of the original condition of creation and transformation, it is therefore said that transformation is accomplished without a deliberate mind. These sayings of Master Cheng each have their appropriate application. How could they contradict one another? Speaking in terms of a bright mirror reflecting things, it is therefore said that when the heart has a governing focus, it is empty; speaking in terms of defending a dilapidated house against raiders, it is therefore said that when the heart has a governing focus, it is full. These sayings of Master Cheng each have a particular referent. How could he deliberately have been inconsistent?

title: 成化十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
功於學者比之荀卿所謂養心莫善於誠
蓋不惟不知盡心且不識所謂誠霄壤不
侔矣程子以心使心則可之說體用之謂
不欲學者縱其心之自由也較之釋氏所
謂以心觀心蓋欲以此一心觀彼一心氷
炭不相同矣顏子之違仁微有間斷耳豈
私意未忘者可擬倫哉明道之獵心偶然
之喜耳豈玩物喪志者可同語哉愚也潜
心孔孟之學反復經傳之旨蓋亦有年矣
===
心齋坐忘固未敢上希於顏子涵養用敬
願致力於程子之言以終身焉若夫心通
乎道然後能辨是非如持權衡以較輕重
是則所謂知言愚生何足以與此惟執事

功於學者。比之荀卿所謂「養心莫善於誠」，蓋不惟不知盡心，且不識所謂誠，霄壤不侔矣。程子「以心使心則可」之說，體用之謂，不欲學者縱其心之自由也。較之釋氏所謂「以心觀心」，蓋欲以此一心觀彼一心，氷炭不相同矣。顏子之違仁，微有間斷耳，豈私意未忘者可擬倫哉？明道之獵心，偶然之喜耳，豈玩物喪志者可同語哉？愚也潜心孔孟之學，反復經傳之旨，蓋亦有年矣。心齋坐忘，固未敢上希於顏子；涵養用敬，願致力於程子之言，以終身焉。若夫心通乎道，然後能辨是非，如持權衡以較輕重，是則所謂知言，愚生何足以與此？惟執事先生幸進教之。

translation_en:
…has greatly benefited students. Compare this with Xun Qing’s statement, “In nourishing the mind, nothing is better than sincerity”: Xun Qing not only failed to understand fully developing the mind, but did not even recognize what sincerity means. The two are as far apart as heaven and earth. Master Cheng’s statement, “Using the mind to direct the mind is permissible,” refers to substance and function; he did not want students to let their minds follow their own inclinations unchecked. Compare this with the Buddhists’ so-called “using the mind to observe the mind”: they would have this mind observe another mind. The two are as incompatible as ice and burning charcoal.

Master Yan’s departures from humaneness were merely slight interruptions. How could those who have not relinquished selfish intentions be compared with him? Mingdao’s impulse to hunt was merely a momentary delight. How could he be spoken of in the same terms as those who lose their resolve through indulgence in things? For my part, I have devoted myself to the learning of Confucius and Mencius and repeatedly pondered the purport of the classics and their commentaries for some years now. As for “fasting of the mind” and “sitting in forgetfulness,” I certainly do not yet dare aspire to Master Yan’s heights. In nurturing the mind through reverent attentiveness, however, I wish to devote myself to Master Cheng’s words throughout my life. As for the mind’s attaining communion with the Way and only then being able to distinguish right from wrong, like weighing light and heavy on a balance—this is what is called “understanding words.” How could an ignorant student such as I be qualified to attain this? I ask only that you, honored sir, kindly instruct me.

考試官侍講李批：子之論事正矣！將用之日，人亦將於子乎觀，勉之哉！
考試官洗馬羅批：詳贍之文，歸於至當，五策中有史學者。
事之在天下，有異勢而同理者，有同行而異情者，惟在公私之間焉。出於公，則雖異，不害其為同；出於私，則雖同，適所以為異。比事而觀之，據理而定之，而君子小人之情見矣。執事發策諸生，詢以古人之事，皆有官守者之職，而愚也非其職也。然言及之而不言，可乎？陳平錢穀决獄之對，非以宰相為無所為也，總其大而不侵其細耳。而德宗以吏禮委張延賞，刑法委柳渾，是
translation_en:
…After three sighs of admiration, I wipe my eyes in anticipation of what he will accomplish.
Associate Examiner Fang, Instructor, comments: This policy essay excels at discussing the ancients. It examines the traces of their conduct and probes the subtleties of their underlying intentions. Its judgments are firmly grounded and entirely apt: this is a scholar of extensive learning, discernment, and breadth of mind. When he takes his place at court one day, would he willingly betray what he has learned?
Examiner Li, Expositor, comments: Your judgments on affairs are correct! When the day comes for you to put them into practice, others will in turn watch you. Exert yourself!
Examiner Luo, Librarian of the Heir Apparent, comments: Detailed and ample writing that arrives at thoroughly sound conclusions. Among the five policy essays, this one displays historical learning.
Among affairs in the world, some differ in circumstances yet share the same principle; others involve the same conduct yet differ in underlying motives. The distinction lies solely between public-mindedness and private interest. When actions arise from public-mindedness, differences do not prevent their being fundamentally alike; when they arise from private interest, their very similarity serves to reveal their difference. Compare the events and examine them; judge them according to principle. Then the true motives of the gentleman and the petty man become apparent. You, honored examiners, have set policy questions for the candidates, asking about the affairs of the ancients. These all concern the duties of men holding official responsibilities, whereas I, in my ignorance, hold no such office. Yet, since these matters have been raised, could I remain silent?
Chen Ping’s reply concerning revenue in money and grain and the adjudication of legal cases did not mean that a chief councilor had nothing to do. He merely oversaw the larger concerns without encroaching on the details. But Dezong entrusted personnel and ritual affairs to Zhang Yanshang, and penal law to Liu Hun; this was…

title: 成化十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
分之也故李泌以為不可分曹參清靜寧
壹之治非以宰相為無所事也守其成而
勿失其舊耳而昭烈在蜀漢草創之時吳
魏未平之日是無所承也故諸葛亮雖勞
而不為變白去副封者非魏相之防壅蔽
乎而疏有不可輒焚之而不上聞趙普之
身任天下殆不可與壅蔽者同科也不為
密啓者非李沆之惡讒佞乎而才有可為
必先啓而後顯奏山濤之擇才授任固不
===
可與讒佞者例論也願從逄干朱雲之直
諫不顧身也魏徵之願為臯夔者則以成
其美於君徵豈不能諫諍者哉桃李在門
狄仁傑之薦賢非為私也王曾之未嘗顯
拔則以歸其恩於上曾豈不能薦賢者哉
之數人者以愛君憂國為心不必其言言
之皆合以居官盡職為務不必其事事之
皆類豈非所謂異而同者乎張安世每定
大政雖大臣莫知其與議其慎密可重也

punctuated: 分之也，故李泌以為不可分。曹參清靜寧壹之治，非以宰相為無所事也，守其成而勿失其舊耳。而昭烈在蜀漢草創之時、吳魏未平之日，是無所承也，故諸葛亮雖勞而不為變。白去副封者，非魏相之防壅蔽乎？而疏有不可，輒焚之而不上聞，趙普之身任天下，殆不可與壅蔽者同科也。不為密啓者，非李沆之惡讒佞乎？而才有可為，必先啓而後顯奏，山濤之擇才授任，固不可與讒佞者例論也。願從逄干朱雲之直，諫不顧身也；魏徵之願為臯夔者，則以成其美於君，徵豈不能諫諍者哉？桃李在門，狄仁傑之薦賢，非為私也；王曾之未嘗顯拔，則以歸其恩於上，曾豈不能薦賢者哉？之數人者，以愛君憂國為心，不必其言言之皆合；以居官盡職為務，不必其事事之皆類。豈非所謂異而同者乎？張安世每定大政，雖大臣莫知其與議，其慎密可重也。
translation_en:
…this divided their responsibilities; hence Li Mi held that they should not be divided. Cao Can’s government of quietude and tranquility did not mean that a chief councilor had nothing to do: he merely preserved what had been accomplished without abandoning established practices. But Emperor Zhaolie was in Shu Han when the state was newly founded and Wu and Wei had yet to be subdued. There was thus no established order to inherit, so Zhuge Liang’s strenuous exertions did not constitute a departure from principle.

Was it not to prevent obstruction of the ruler’s access to information that Wei Xiang requested the abolition of duplicate sealed copies of memorials? Yet Zhao Pu, whenever he found a memorial unacceptable, would burn it without bringing it to the ruler’s attention. In personally assuming responsibility for the realm, Zhao Pu can hardly be placed in the same category as those who obstruct the ruler’s access to information. Was it not because Li Hang detested slander and flattery that he refrained from submitting confidential reports? Yet whenever Shan Tao found someone whose talents could be put to use, he invariably reported privately first and then submitted a public recommendation. In selecting talented men and assigning them office, he certainly cannot be discussed on the same footing as slanderers and flatterers.

To wish to emulate the forthrightness of Longfeng and Bi Gan [?; transcribed as 逄干] and Zhu Yun was to remonstrate without regard for one’s own life. Wei Zheng’s wish to become like Gao Yao and Kui, however, was intended to bring his ruler’s virtues to perfection. Could Zheng possibly have been incapable of remonstrance? With ‘peach and plum trees at his gate’—the worthy men he had recommended—Di Renjie did not recommend talent for private advantage. Wang Zeng, however, never openly promoted anyone, so that the credit for such favor would accrue to his sovereign. Could Zeng possibly have been incapable of recommending worthy men?

These several men [?; transcribed as 之數人者] took love for their ruler and concern for the state to heart; their every utterance did not have to agree. They made fulfilling their official duties their task; their every action did not have to be alike. Were they not examples of what is called being different yet the same? Whenever Zhang Anshi helped settle major policies, even the high ministers did not know that he had participated in the deliberations. His discretion deserves esteem.

title: 成化十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
而孔光兄弟燕語不及朝省政事彼固持
佐保祿之人耳何取焉裴度之獨定大策
雖舉朝莫能奪其果斷可稱也而王安石
力主新法謂人言不足恤者彼固愎諫遂
非之人耳何責焉姚崇之拜宰相也以十
事堅玄宗之志其意則主於得行若秦檜
三奏高宗而後議和者適以成天下之患
而已蕭望之為郡守以一疏而還少府之
官其意則主於重內若丁謂入謝願留而
===
復入相者徒以固一時之位而已公孫弘
為汲黯所論乃服罪於布被之詐而反稱
其忠取重武帝者愈足以見其詐王旦為
冦準所短乃引過於政府之闕而益稱其
直取重真宗者愈足以彰其美朝廷欲用
程頤則曰頤入恐不肯靜此蘇轍之言非
所以快私忿乎洛蜀之辨轍盖有不能容
頤者矣諫官欲引石介則曰介必以難事
責君也范仲淹之言非所以顧國體乎伏

寇準所短乃引過於政府之關而益稱其

公孫弘為汲黯所論，乃服罪於布被之詐，而反稱其忠，取重武帝者，愈足以見其詐。王旦為冦準所短，乃引過於政府之闕，而益稱其直，取重真宗者，愈足以彰其美。朝廷欲用程頤，則曰：「頤入恐不肯靜。」此蘇轍之言，非所以快私忿乎？洛蜀之辨，轍盖有不能容頤者矣。諫官欲引石介，則曰：「介必以難事責君也。」范仲淹之言，非所以顧國體乎？伏
translation_en:
…Yet when Kong Guang conversed informally with his brothers, he never touched upon affairs of court or government. He was merely a man intent on maintaining his position [?] and preserving his stipend. What was there to admire in him? Pei Du alone settled a major policy, and even the entire court could not deflect him: his decisiveness deserves praise. Yet Wang Anshi vigorously championed the New Policies and declared that others’ criticisms need cause no concern. He was merely a man who obstinately rejected remonstrance and persisted in error. What could one expect of him? When Yao Chong was appointed chief councilor, he used ten proposals to secure Emperor Xuanzong’s resolve; his purpose was to ensure that his policies could be carried out. By contrast, Qin Hui’s submitting three memorials to Emperor Gaozong before negotiating peace merely brought calamity upon the realm. When Xiao Wangzhi was a commandery governor, a single memorial secured his return to the office of Chamberlain for Palace Revenues; his purpose was to give due weight to service at the central court. By contrast, Ding Wei’s entering court to offer thanks, requesting to remain, and subsequently returning as chief councilor merely secured his position for the moment.
When Ji An criticized Gongsun Hong, Hong admitted his fault in deceptively using a plain cloth coverlet, but then praised Ji An’s loyalty, thereby gaining Emperor Wu’s esteem. This only further exposed his deceit. When Kou Zhun criticized Wang Dan’s shortcomings, Wang accepted responsibility for deficiencies in the chief councilors’ administration and praised Kou’s uprightness all the more, thereby gaining Emperor Zhenzong’s esteem. This only further demonstrated his virtue. When the court wished to employ Cheng Yi, Su Zhe said, “If Yi enters court, I fear he will not be willing to remain quiet.” Were these words not a means of gratifying a private resentment? In the dispute between the Luo and Shu factions, Zhe apparently could not tolerate Yi. When a remonstrance official wished to recommend Shi Jie, Fan Zhongyan said, “Jie will certainly demand difficult things of his sovereign.” Were Fan Zhongyan’s words not intended to safeguard the dignity of the state? 是非所謂同而異者乎噫甚矣君子小人
之難辨也曲直之不易分也彼以為是此

translation_en: …the remonstrance at the palace gates: Zhongyan indeed had compelling reasons for his stance toward Jie. Of these men, some took accommodating measures to accomplish public business, while others used pretexts to advance private interests. Viewed in their outward conduct, they are as easily confused as vermilion and purple; examined in their hearts, they are as opposed as ice and burning charcoal. Is this not what is meant by being alike yet different? Alas! How very difficult it is to distinguish the gentleman from the petty man, and how hard to separate wrong from right! What one considers right, another considers wrong; what one considers crooked, another considers upright. Without the impartial judgment of all under Heaven, who could settle the matter? Nevertheless, the rights and wrongs of the latter several men need no further discussion. Concerning the former several men, I venture to offer my own view. A gentleman must understand how Li Mi discharged the duties of chief councilor before he can discuss Chen Ping’s grasp of the essentials; he must understand how Zhuge exhausted himself in service before he can discuss Cao Can’s preservation of established achievements. Better to be loyal like Wei Xiang than to imitate Zhao Pu’s conduct to the point of rejecting remonstrance; better to be forthright like Zhu Yun than to follow Wei Zheng’s arguments to the point of compromising one’s integrity. Only when all one’s recommendations are appropriate, like those submitted by Shan Tao, may one cease to adhere rigidly to Li Hang’s words; only when all those one recommends are worthy, like those recommended by Di Renjie, may one cease to be bound by Wang Zeng’s admonition. Seek only to keep one’s heart unwavering, without judging by outward appearances; seek only to remain true to moral principle, without calculating other considerations. Confucius said: “Choose what is good in them and follow it; take what is not good in them and correct it in yourself.” These men are all my teachers. As for me, in…

執事之問而得師焉輒復盡其狂斐惟與

第四問
徐元獻
同考試官訓導鄺批本房暗經義論策皆
固多某場可觀者盼學校科目一策以為條答詳贍故

之所負矣雖非伯樂寧不為子一顧邪
===

風簷寸晷之下不足以得士乎
考試官洗馬羅批答既無遺論亦合體置之

沐菁莪教雨之化者知學校為育材之盛
地聽鹿鳴燕饗之歌者知科目為取士之
正途然必考於古乃可見古人之盛不識
於今又何以知

第四問
徐元獻

同考試官訓導鄺批：「本房暗經義論策皆固多某場可觀者，盼學校科目一策，以為條答詳贍，故錄之。」

同考試官學正梁批：「觀子今日之答，足見子之所負矣。雖非伯樂，寧不為子一顧邪？」

考試官洗馬羅批：「答既無遺，論亦合體，置之前列，足以自見矣。」

宋之良法而行之有以也
今日輔理承化庶司百府之賢胥此焉出誠
有如執事之言也請條陳之學校之建所
以明人倫而教養英才也昔成周之教自
一年視離經辨志及乎論學取友是之謂
小成至九年知類通達強立不反是之謂

translation_en:
…There is good reason why our dynasty honors Confucian learning, establishes schools and examination categories, and weighs and implements the sound institutions of the Three Dynasties and of the Han, Tang, and Song. Today, the worthy men who assist in government and carry forward its transforming influence throughout the many offices and bureaus all emerge from these institutions. It is indeed as you, sir, have said. Allow me to set out the particulars.
Schools are established to clarify human relationships and to educate and nurture outstanding talent. In former times, under the educational system of the Zhou, students were first assessed after one year on their ability to divide the Classics into meaningful passages and distinguish their aspirations. When they reached the stage of discussing learning and choosing friends, this was called “minor attainment.” By the ninth year, they understood categories and their connections, stood firmly on their own, and did not fall back: this was called “major attainment.” Those who would not follow the teachings were first transferred to the suburbs, next to the outer districts, and then banished to distant regions, excluded from recognized standing for life. These regulations were fully developed. Although later dynasties such as the Han, Tang, and Song did not equal this, no age lacked capable teachers. Under the Han, Huan Rong elucidated the meaning of the Classics with a clarity unmatched by other scholars; Dai Ping was inexhaustible in explaining the Classics and was summoned and appointed a Gentleman. Under the Tang, there was Yang Cheng, whose conduct provided a standard and whose words and actions were emulated; there was also Bao Mou [?], who encouraged good and checked wrongdoing, and was sincere, kindly, and amiable. All were outstanding Confucian teachers. What gentlemen esteemed was simply Huan Rong’s investigation of antiquity and Yang Cheng’s steadfast integrity. In the Song, Master Hu of Anding, when teaching in Suzhou and Huzhou, maintained a Hall of Classical Meaning to teach the learning that illuminates fundamental principles, and a Hall of Practical Affairs to develop talent suited to practical use. … a master of Confucian learning [?]?
The examination categories were established in order to gather … [five illegible characters]…

text:

所謂造士有所謂選士又有所謂進士而

…came forth from this. In former times, the perfected Zhou taught three categories of things. The first was the six virtues: wisdom, benevolence, sagacity, righteousness, loyalty, and harmony. The second was the six forms of conduct: filial devotion, brotherly affection, concord with one's kin, amity with relatives by marriage, dependability, and compassion. The third was the six arts: ritual, music, archery, charioteering, writing, and mathematics. The worthy and capable were honored as guests and recommended for advancement. There were those called “fully trained scholars” (zaoshi), those called “selected scholars” (xuanshi), and also those called “presented scholars” (jinshi); their abilities were distinguished and assessed. The system was complete. Later dynasties such as the Han, Tang, and Song did not attain this standard, yet their systems of selection never lacked outstanding men. Kuang Heng, whose explanations of the Book of Odes brought delighted smiles and who submitted forthright memorials on affairs of state, and Xiao Wangzhi, whose understanding of the Classics, steadiness, and abilities fitted him to serve as chief councilor, were eminent under the Han. Under the Tang, Han Changli was renowned for rejecting Buddhism and Daoism and for being as the mountain and the Dipper in literary achievement; Lu Jingyu was renowned for discussing benevolence and righteousness in his remonstrances and for living up to his learning. All were outstanding among those selected for their worth. What gentlemen admired in them was simply Han's “Tracing the Way to Its Source” (Yuan dao) and Lu's loyalty to his sovereign. In the Song, Master Zhu, known as Hui'an, proposed in his “Personal Views on Tribute Recommendation” (Gongju siyi) that the various Classics be examined in different years and that the histories be studied alongside the Classics. Was this not a consummate discussion of examination and recommendation?
We reverently reflect that our dynasty studies antiquity, honors literary learning, esteems Confucian scholars, and gives weight to the Way. In establishing schools, it has left no distant region or remote town without one, and no person in even the humblest dwelling without learning. It has selected learned Confucian teachers to take sole charge of instruction and has also ordered censorial officials to supervise its overall direction. Its establishment of regulations and provisions truly embodies the admirable intention of putting conduct before literary learning. 事于佔畢，豈足以教士？然則一於此固不可，遂舎此亦不可。惟當申明人倫，率先禮義，弱者養之以至於剛，虚者養之以至於充，伸於久屈之中，而用於至足之後，流於既溢之餘，而發於持滿之末。又時放乎安定蘇湖之教焉，則雖勸懲於文藝，亦足以驗進修，將不有明體適用者興於其間乎？
其設科也，當三年而大比，有司為之勸駕。諸藩則分聘儒學之官以司試事，兩京則特命翰苑之臣以重文衡。登進考校，亦鄉舉里選之遺意也。使司此法者但糊名而已，易書而已，解額而已，以取人於一日之試，豈足以待士？然則一於此誠不可，遂舎此亦不可。惟當試之以法言，考之以實學，博通經術者雖樸不廢，稍涉浮誕者雖工必黜，則風俗雅厚，學術近正。又兼取乎悔菴貢舉之議焉，則雖校量乎文墨，亦足以為□
translation_en:
… occupy themselves with textual recitation—how could this suffice to educate scholars? To concentrate exclusively on this is certainly unacceptable, yet abandoning it altogether is equally unacceptable. Rather, one should elucidate human relationships and take the lead in ritual propriety and righteousness, nurturing the weak until they become strong and the empty until they become full. Their capacities should unfold after long restraint and be put to use only after becoming fully sufficient; they should flow only once filled to overflowing and find expression only after their fullness has been sustained. If one also periodically models instruction on the teaching of Anding [Hu Yuan] at Suzhou and Huzhou, then even encouragement and correction through literary composition will suffice to assess progress in learning and self-cultivation. Will there not then arise among them men who understand fundamental principles and can apply them in practice?
As for the establishment of examinations, a great examination is held every three years, and the responsible officials encourage candidates to proceed to it. In the provinces, officials of the Confucian schools are separately engaged to oversee the examinations; in the two capitals, officials of the Hanlin Academy are specially appointed by imperial command to lend weight to literary adjudication. Such advancement and assessment also preserve the intention of the ancient practice of recommending men from the townships and selecting them from the villages. If those administering this system do no more than seal candidates’ names, have their scripts recopied, and observe provincial graduate quotas, selecting men through a single day’s examination, how could this suffice to treat scholars properly? To concentrate exclusively on this is indeed unacceptable, yet abandoning it altogether is equally unacceptable. Rather, one should test them through exemplary discourse and assess them for substantive learning. Those broadly versed in classical learning should not be rejected even if their writing is plain; those whose work is even slightly frivolous or extravagant must be rejected, however polished it may be. Customs will then become refined and generous, and learning will approach what is correct. If one also adopts the proposals on recruitment by examination made by Hui’an [?; apparently an error for Zhu Xi’s sobriquet, Hui’an 晦菴], then even assessment through written compositions will suffice to serve as □ …

… standards. Would there not then emerge among them men of flourishing talent and exceptional ability? This is what you, gentlemen charged with this examination, ought to attend to today. As for nurturing talent in the schools, the responsible officials have already provided regular instruction and cultivated it beforehand. Surely there are now proud herds of steeds from northern Ji awaiting a single appreciative glance from Bo Le? Black or yellow, mare or stallion—the choice rests with you. Respectfully submitted.

Fifth Question
Han Bi

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Instructor: Those who answer questions on current affairs are often vague and lack a central argument. This paper takes securing worthy men as its theme. Its extended exposition flows freely, its reasoning is clear, and its meaning is fully conveyed. Its author must surely be a man fit for high service, like a precious sacrificial vessel.

Comment by Associate Examiner Fang, Instructor: This policy essay on troops and provisions displays remarkably firm judgments. Those who understand the affairs of their time are outstanding men. Might you be such a man?

Comment by Examiner Li, Expositor: His arguments are balanced and sound; he is a man of useful talent. Finding this at the end of the policy-essay examination made me so happy that I could not sleep.

Comment by Examiner Luo, Librarian: He has mature judgments and makes no rash statements. With aspirations and abilities such as these, he merits recommendation.

title: 成化十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
可以臻久安之治為士者講之於窮居之
日則可以為待用之資凡天下之事皆然
而況其大者乎愚非經濟才也然於此亦
嘗究心焉耳矣執事不以為愚而問之願
陳其說古者寓兵於農其後寓農於兵又
其後也籍農以為兵
國朝酌古定制民出食以養兵而兵無不足
兵出力以衛民而民無不安誠萬世不易
之法今版圖之內黔黎極總總之繁囷庾
之間穀粟有陳陳之積食非不足也被堅
執銳者洸洸乎江漢之英折衝禦侮者赳
赳乎燕趙之傑兵非不足也於其足而益
求其足則亦有說焉蘇松之郡舊多良田
而賦固加厚故常賦之外猶有餘資今耗
數之加至於倍蓰私貸之息復累歲年何
恠乎民之闕賦也使糧耗有定制而不浮
貸息有常數而不過困者其少蘇乎滄瀛
諸郡舊多閒田而賦又甚薄故恒產之外

可以臻久安之治。為士者講之於窮居之日，則可以為待用之資。凡天下之事皆然，而況其大者乎？愚非經濟才也，然於此亦嘗究心焉耳矣。執事不以為愚而問之，願陳其說。古者寓兵於農，其後寓農於兵，又其後也籍農以為兵。
國朝酌古定制，民出食以養兵，而兵無不足；兵出力以衛民，而民無不安。誠萬世不易之法。今版圖之內，黔黎極總總之繁；囷庾之間，穀粟有陳陳之積。食非不足也。被堅執銳者，洸洸乎江漢之英；折衝禦侮者，赳赳乎燕趙之傑。兵非不足也。於其足而益求其足，則亦有說焉。蘇松之郡，舊多良田，而賦固加厚，故常賦之外，猶有餘資。今耗數之加，至於倍蓰；私貸之息，復累歲年。何恠乎民之闕賦也？使糧耗有定制而不浮，貸息有常數而不過，困者其少蘇乎？滄瀛諸郡，舊多閒田，而賦又甚薄，故恒產之外，
translation_en:
…can bring about enduring peace and order. If scholars study these matters while living in obscurity, they can equip themselves for future service. This holds true of all affairs under Heaven; how much more so of the greatest among them! I have no talent for ordering the state and aiding its people, yet I have devoted some thought to these matters. Since you, sir, have not dismissed me as foolish but have asked my views, I wish to set them forth. In antiquity, soldiers were incorporated among the farmers; later, farming was incorporated into the army; and later still, farmers were registered for military service.
Our dynasty weighed ancient precedents and established its institutions: the people provide food to support the soldiers, so that the soldiers lack nothing; the soldiers exert their strength to protect the people, so that all the people enjoy security. This is indeed a system that should remain unchanged for ten thousand generations. Today, within the realm, the common people are exceedingly numerous, and in the granaries grain is piled up, old stores upon old stores. Food is certainly not insufficient. Those who wear armor and wield sharp weapons are the martial heroes of the Jiang and Han regions; those who repel attacks and resist aggression are the valiant outstanding men of Yan and Zhao. Soldiers are certainly not insufficient. Yet there is something to be said about seeking still greater sufficiency where sufficiency already exists. The prefectures of Suzhou and Songjiang formerly had much fertile farmland. Although their taxes were correspondingly heavy, resources still remained after payment of the regular levy. Now additional grain-loss surcharges have risen to two or five times the amount, while interest on private loans accumulates year after year. Why be surprised that the people fall short in paying their taxes? If grain-loss surcharges were fixed by regulation and not inflated, and interest on loans had an established rate that was not exceeded, might those in distress gain some relief? The prefectures of Cang and Ying formerly had much unused land, and their taxes were also very light; thus, beyond their established holdings, …

title: 成化十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
猶有餘地今雜泛之役丁口無遺兼并之
家阡陌相望何惑乎民之無田也使用有
節則徭役可以少減籍有定則兼并可以
寢消貧者其少安乎今
朝廷之於民也有賑貸之法有勸借之法有
儲蓄之法所以念之者至矣然里胥點猾
則貧者不得以自通官吏刻深則富室困
之而俱敝考覈未實則簿籍雖有而徒存
其在郡縣愚不敢謂無也是非奉法者之
===
或非其人乎使守令皆賢則政務畢舉不
但此三者而已然就三者論之則儲蓄為
尤重蓋必積之於充溢之餘而後可濟之
於闕乏之際不必賑貸也而上下皆足不
必勸借也而貧富自均民既足矣雖有水
旱之至不足以害吾治況未必有乎蠻夷
之在嶺海者固已革心向化於
聖治之中無復向之睢盱矣然欲使之萬世而
無虞者則治之有若稂莠然勤耕耘以除

之而俱敝考覈未實則簿籍雖有而徒存
具在郡縣愚不敢謂無也是非奉法者之
===
咸非其人乎使守令皆賢則政務畢舉不
但此三者而已然就三者論之則儲蓄爲
尤重蓋必積之於充溢之餘而後可濟之
於闕乏之際不必賑貸也而上下皆足不
必勸借也而貧富自均民蓋足矣雖有水
旱之至不足以害吾治况未必有乎蠻夷
之在嶺海者固已革心向化於
聖治之中無復向之雖肝矣然欲使之萬世而
無虞者則治之有若根莠然勤耕耘深除
punctuated:
猶有餘地。今雜泛之役，丁口無遺；兼并之家，阡陌相望。何惑乎民之無田也？使用有節，則徭役可以少減；籍有定，則兼并可以寢消。貧者其少安乎？今朝廷之於民也，有賑貸之法，有勸借之法，有儲蓄之法，所以念之者至矣。然里胥點猾，則貧者不得以自通；官吏刻深，則富室困之而俱敝；考覈未實，則簿籍雖有而徒存。其在郡縣，愚不敢謂無也。是非奉法者之或非其人乎？使守令皆賢，則政務畢舉，不但此三者而已。然就三者論之，則儲蓄為尤重。蓋必積之於充溢之餘，而後可濟之於闕乏之際。不必賑貸也，而上下皆足；不必勸借也，而貧富自均。民既足矣，雖有水旱之至，不足以害吾治，況未必有乎？
蠻夷之在嶺海者，固已革心向化，於聖治之中，無復向之睢盱矣。然欲使之萬世而無虞者，則治之有若稂莠然，勤耕耘以除
translation_en:
…there was still land to spare. Now miscellaneous labor services leave no adult male or other registered person untouched, while the fields of households that engross land stretch as far as the eye can see. Why be puzzled that the people have no land? If demands upon their service were restrained, labor obligations could be somewhat reduced; if registers were firmly established, land engrossment could gradually subside. Might the poor then enjoy a little peace?
The court now has provisions for relief loans, for encouraging loans from the wealthy, and for building reserves. Its solicitude for the people is most thorough. Yet when village clerks are unscrupulous and cunning [?], the poor cannot make their needs known; when officials are harsh and exacting, wealthy households are burdened, and all alike are impoverished; when scrutiny is not grounded in fact, registers exist only in name. I would not venture to say that such things do not occur in prefectures and counties. Is this not because some of those charged with enforcing the laws are unsuited to their duties? If prefects and magistrates were all worthy, every governmental task would be carried out, not merely these three measures. Yet among these three, building reserves is especially important. Only by accumulating supplies when there is abundance can one provide relief when shortages arise. Then, without needing relief loans, those above and below would all have enough; without needing to encourage loans from the wealthy, the resources of rich and poor would naturally be balanced. Once the people have enough, even floods and droughts would be insufficient to damage our good government—how much more so when such disasters may never occur!
The non-Han peoples in the Linghai region have already changed their hearts and turned toward civilizing influence. Under sagely rule, they no longer glare defiantly as before. Yet to ensure that they pose no cause for concern for ten thousand generations, one must govern them as one deals with weeds, diligently plowing and hoeing to remove…

title: 成化十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
穡在我有以擇之而已夫何憂戎虜之在
沙漠者罔已破膽喪氣於
天威之下無敢昔之跳梁矣然欲使之萬世而
無警者則馭之有若禽獸然嚴藩籬備械
器在我有以制之而已夫何慮今
朝廷之於兵有肄練之法有勾稽之法有給
養之法所以重乎兵者至矣然玩愒於恬
熈之化者作止或未齊逋亡於掊克之私
者行伍或未實侵削於並緣之弊者衣食
===
或未充其在邊鄙愚不敢謂無也是非奉
職者之或非其人乎將領皆賢則兵政悉
備不止此三者而已然就此三者言之則給
養為尤重盖必使安於食飽力足之娛而
後可倡其投石超距之勇由是而肄練其
所未習則人懷敵愾之心由是而勾稽其
所未實則士知行伍之樂兵益足矣雖有
外警之至不足以妨吾治況不足慮乎然
堯之水湯之旱周之玁狁皆不能無故當

柚在我有以禦之而已夫何夏戎虜之在
沙漠者固已破膽寒心於
天威之下無敢肯之跳梁然欲建之萬世而
無警者則馭之有若禽獸然嚴藩籬備積
儲在我有以制之而已夫何慮今
朝廷之於兵有肄練之法有勾稽之法有給
養之法所以重乎兵者至矣然猶慮於悟
興之化者作止或未齊進退於格免之私
者行伍或未實侵削於盈縮之弊者衣食
===
或未充其在邊郡愚不敢謂無也是推奉
職者之或非其人乎將領皆賢則兵政悉
備不止此三者而已然就三者言之則給
養為允重蓋必使其於食飽力足之娛而
後可倡其奮厲超距之勇由是而肄練其
所未習則人懷敵愾之心由是而勾稽其
所未實則士知行伍之樂兵益足矣雖有
外警之至不足以妨吾治況不足慮乎然
堯之水湯之旱周之獵狁皆不能無故當
punctuated:
穡，在我有以擇之而已，夫何憂？戎虜之在沙漠者，罔已破膽喪氣於天威之下，無敢昔之跳梁矣。然欲使之萬世而無警者，則馭之有若禽獸然，嚴藩籬，備械器，在我有以制之而已，夫何慮？
今朝廷之於兵，有肄練之法，有勾稽之法，有給養之法，所以重乎兵者至矣。然玩愒於恬熈之化者，作止或未齊；逋亡於掊克之私者，行伍或未實；侵削於並緣之弊者，衣食或未充。其在邊鄙，愚不敢謂無也。是非奉職者之或非其人乎？將領皆賢，則兵政悉備，不止此三者而已。然就此三者言之，則給養為尤重。盖必使安於食飽力足之娛，而後可倡其投石超距之勇。由是而肄練其所未習，則人懷敵愾之心；由是而勾稽其所未實，則士知行伍之樂。兵益足矣，雖有外警之至，不足以妨吾治，況不足慮乎？然堯之水、湯之旱、周之玁狁，皆不能無，故當
translation_en:
…the crops [?]; we need only have the means to select among them—what cause is there for anxiety? The Rong enemies in the desert have already [?] lost their courage and spirit before imperial might and no longer dare to run rampant as they once did. Yet to ensure that they cause no alarms for ten thousand generations, we must control them as we would birds and beasts: strengthen the fences and prepare weapons and equipment. We need only have the means to restrain them—what cause is there for concern?
As for the court’s treatment of the troops today, there are methods for training, methods for checking the rolls, and methods for provisioning. The importance accorded to the troops could scarcely be greater. Yet among those who idle away their time under this peaceful rule, movements and halts may not be coordinated; because men flee private extortion, the ranks may not be full; and because abuses afford opportunities for embezzlement, clothing and food may be insufficient. I would not venture to say that such things do not occur on the frontiers. Is this not because some of those charged with these duties are unsuitable men? If the commanders are all worthy, military administration will be complete in every respect, extending beyond these three matters alone. Yet of these three, provisioning is especially important. The men must first enjoy the comfort of full stomachs and ample strength; only then can their prowess in throwing stones and leaping distances be encouraged. With this foundation, train them in what they have not yet mastered, and every man will cherish the resolve to confront the enemy; with this foundation, check the rolls wherever the ranks are under strength, and the soldiers will know the satisfaction of military service. Military resources will become still more ample. Even if an external alarm should arise, it will not be enough to impede our governance; how much less, then, need it cause concern? Yet even the floods of Yao’s time, the drought of Tang’s time, and the Xianyun incursions under the Zhou could not be wholly avoided. Thus, when…

title: 成化十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
烝民乃粒之時而大禹陳艱食之戒當九
功惟敘之日而臯陶明屢省之言則兵食
之政正
聖世之所當講也愚不敢自棄敢因執事之問
以守令將帥為言若黜幽陟明激勤懲惰
則
廟堂之事非草茅之賤可得而與也倘因執
事而有聞焉亦豈獨斯言之幸也哉謹對

translation_en: …when the multitudes had grain to eat, Yu the Great set forth his warning about the difficulty of securing food; when the nine achievements were duly ordered, Gao Yao made clear the need for repeated scrutiny. Thus military affairs and food supplies are precisely the matters that should be examined in this age of sage rule. Ignorant though I am, I dare not abandon my responsibility, and so, in response to your question, I have ventured to speak of prefects and magistrates, generals and commanders. As for dismissing the unworthy and promoting the worthy, encouraging diligence and punishing indolence, these are matters for the imperial court, in which a lowly man outside official service cannot presume to participate. If, through you, these words should reach those above, would the good fortune be confined to these words alone? Respectfully submitted in reply.

translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination

On the guiyou day of the eighth month, in autumn of the gengzi year, the sixteenth year of Chenghua [1480], the Record of the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination was completed. Twenty-six days elapsed between receipt of the imperial edict and the first examination session. Three days later came the second session, and another three days later the third. The work was concluded eleven days after the examinations. The record was then compiled, listing thirty-six officials of the central and local administrations assigned to examination duties, the 135 candidates selected, and twenty especially fine essays. title: 成化十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
姓舜始五服文王始周南者
地之近也近必先久則益以
深故天下莫加焉臣嘗以為
西北之人才京畿為盛東南
之人才南畿為盛蓋嘗觀于
南矣仰惟我
太祖高皇帝盛德大業之所興一
===
時雄才傑士建功立名之所
起靈氣在山川風霆雨露在
萬物
仁聲義烈之在遺民故老者昭
然如一日
太宗文皇帝定都于北
宮闕臺署兩存而並置以為億

translation_en: …clans; Shun began with the five zones of submission, and King Wen began with the lands of the “Airs of Zhou and the South,” because these places were near at hand. What is near must come first; with time, the influence grows ever deeper, so that nowhere else in the realm surpasses it. Your servant has long considered that talent in the northwest flourishes most abundantly in the capital region, and talent in the southeast in the southern capital region. Indeed, I have observed the south myself. Reverently I reflect that it was here that our Emperor Taizu Gao’s abundant virtue and great enterprise arose, and here that the outstanding men of his age rose to achieve merit and establish their names. Numinous energy abides in its mountains and rivers; wind, thunder, rain, and dew act upon its myriad things. title: 成化十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
萬載太平之業故人物之魁
傑文章之深厚論議之宏偉
其視沛豐汾晉弓矢甲胄之
雄者相萬也於戲休哉士之
才猷德器必造而後成今國
監在兩京府州縣學徧天下
冠裳絃誦者彬彬輩出非孔
===
孟之學不講非堯舜之道不
求非臯夔伊傅之功業不言
志孚氣感上求而下應取之
乎筆札文字之間而得其精
神心術之妙有不謀而合者
觀于近而天下可知也是又
非

translation_en: … a foundation for enduring peace through myriad ages. Thus, in the outstanding excellence of its men, the depth and substance of its writings, and the grandeur of its discussions, it surpasses ten thousandfold [?] the martial heroes of Pei, Feng, Fen, and Jin, with their bows, arrows, armor, and helmets. Ah, how splendid! Scholars’ talents, judgment, virtue, and capacity must be cultivated before they reach maturity. Today, the Directorate of Education is established in both capitals, and prefectural, subprefectural, and county schools extend throughout the realm. Cultivated men in scholars’ caps and robes, studying through music and recitation, emerge in succession. They expound only the learning of Confucius and Mencius, seek only the Way of Yao and Shun, and speak only of the achievements of Gao Yao, Kui, Yi Yin, and Fu Yue. Their aspirations accord and their vital energies resonate: those above seek talent, and those below respond. title: 成化十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
累朝
列聖偃武修文之化暨我
聖天子甄陶樂育之明效哉然益
以見
皇祖之澤遠矣夫自科舉之法行
天下之願仕者挾經而抱藝
雖遐陬僻壤衡鑑所在皆起
===
而趨之况敎化所始
王畿之近地哉况
天子所命左右侍從之臣以莅乎
其事者哉大則公卿輔相經
邦弘化之功小則諸司百執
事稱德宣力之寄天下所厚
望焉者也盖必保名檢樹功

translation_en: …the manifest effects of the civilizing influence of the sage emperors of successive reigns, who laid aside arms and cultivated civil learning, together with our sage Son of Heaven’s molding and nurturing of talent? Yet this makes still clearer how far the beneficence of the imperial ancestor extends. Ever since the civil-service examination system came into force, all under Heaven who aspire to office have embraced the Classics and cultivated their literary skills. Even in remote corners and secluded districts, wherever talent is assessed, they all rise and hasten toward it. How much more so in this nearby region of the imperial domain, where moral instruction begins! How much more so when the Son of Heaven has appointed ministers who attend at his side to preside over the proceedings! At the higher level, there are the achievements expected of dukes, ministers, and chief councillors in ordering the realm and extending its civilizing influence; at the lower level, there are the responsibilities entrusted to the various offices and their many functionaries to give fitting expression to imperial virtue and exert their strength in service. title: 成化十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
業而後可稱
盛世之才奮志倍力以率先天
下而後可稱
王畿之秀不徒為富貴利達以
為身羞以貽為國者之憂而
後可以稱學校科目之士然
則士之自負于天下亦重矣
===
故相與勗之以觀其成
翰林院侍講李東陽謹序

業，而後可稱盛世之才；奮志倍力，以率先天下，而後可稱王畿之秀；不徒為富貴利達，以為身羞，以貽為國者之憂，而後可以稱學校科目之士。然則士之自負于天下亦重矣。故相與勗之，以觀其成。
翰林院侍講李東陽謹序。
translation_en:
…achievements, and only then can they be called talents of a flourishing age. They must rouse their resolve and redouble their efforts to take the lead throughout the realm; only then can they be called the outstanding men of the metropolitan region. They must not merely pursue wealth, rank, advantage, and advancement, thereby bringing shame upon themselves and causing anxiety to those who govern the state; only then can they be called scholars of the schools and the examination system. Thus the responsibility that scholars themselves bear toward the realm is indeed weighty. We therefore encourage them together and await their accomplishments.
